Root Crops
Artichoke, Jerusalem.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Autumn / Winter

Jerusalem artichokes are not true artichokes at all, but vigorous sunflower relatives grown for their knobbly underground tubers. They are hardy, reliable and useful for winter soups, stews and grated salads, with a sweet, nutty flavour which is not to everybody's taste and may not suit every digestion. The plants grow very tall in rich soil, making them useful as a screen or windbreak but also capable of robbing light from lower crops if planted in a long row. They are easy to grow from tubers, but hard to eradicate once established because even small pieces left in the soil can regrow.

Recommended varieties
Fuseau

Smooth, elongated tubers make this a practical kitchen choice, with less fiddly preparation than very knobbly selections.

Dwarf Sunray

A shorter-growing option with pale, relatively smooth tubers. Worth considering where tall Jerusalem artichokes would be awkward.

Small Wonder

A compact Jerusalem artichoke sold for containers and small plots, with tubers clustered near the stem.

Key risks
SCLEROTINIA ROT

Stem bases rot and may carry fluffy white mould with black, seed-like resting bodies.

SLUGS

Slugs may nibble spring shoots; established Jerusalem artichokes usually outgrow light leaf damage.

MICE

Mice may burrow among tubers in winter and eat stored or unlifted roots.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 1

Growing & harvesting
Choose the site carefully.

Tall stems shade neighbours, and missed tubers regrow readily.

Leave tubers until they are needed.

They are hardy in the ground and provide a useful winter crop.

Soil & preparation
Light, sandy or free-draining soil suits the crop, provided it is not very acid or waterlogged in winter. Improve heavy clay before planting.
Prepare in autumn or early winter, removing perennial weeds and adding compost or well-rotted manure where humus is low. Sandy soil needs less preparation, though compost can improve the crop.
Sowing & planting
1 Set the tuber

Plant tubers in late winter or early spring. Choose a clump or block where tall stems will not shade lower crops.

2 Cover carefully

Cover the tubers carefully and water in. Remove stray tuber fragments when clearing the bed; they can regrow.

Tuber depth 6 in.
Rows 3 ft between rows
Plants / blocks 12 in. between plants
Looking after the crop
Hoe between young plants or mulch deeply to suppress weeds, particularly on heavy ground. Established plants on light soil usually need little attention.
Earth up the bases when stems are about 1 ft tall. Water during dry weather, especially on light soil.
In windy sites, put sturdy canes at the ends of the row and run supporting wires along both sides. Tall stems can also make a temporary windbreak.
Leave flowers for pollinators if desired. Give weak plants an appropriate organic liquid feed during summer.
Harvesting & storage
After the leaves yellow in autumn, cut stems to about 3 in. above the soil. Healthy tops can be used as mulch or woven into a temporary windbreak.
Lift tubers as needed from late autumn through early spring. They are hardy, but frozen ground can prevent access: lift a supply before a hard freeze.
Reserve sound tubers for replanting. Remove unwanted tubers and fragments carefully because even small pieces can regrow.
When clearing a bed, revisit it through spring and repeatedly remove shoots and their tubers. One lifting may not clear the crop completely.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
SCLEROTINIA ROT	White mould and black bodies in rotting stems.	Remove infected plants and debris; avoid spreading affected soil.
SLUGS	Spring leaves nibbled; tubers hollowed.	Inspect and hand-pick; lift mature tubers before damage worsens.
MICE	Tubers are gnawed; tunnels may be present.	Rodent-proof stored tubers and inspect regularly.
Final tips

Keep the tall plants north of shorter vegetables so the screen does not rob them of light.

A manageable clump is often easier to accommodate than a long shading row.

In severe frost, cover stem bases with straw or lift tubers after the tops have died back.

Protect stored tubers from rodents and inspect them regularly for damage or decay.

IMPERIAL · 2

Root Crops
Potato.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Potatoes can feed a household from a small plot, with dense foliage useful on newly prepared ground; check former grassland for wireworms first. They are grown from seed potatoes rather than true seed; the planted tuber produces leafy haulm above ground and new tubers below and near the soil surface. Those tubers must be kept covered, because light turns them green and poisonous. First earlies crop quickly and are useful for fresh new potatoes; second earlies follow; maincrops give higher yields and better winter storage but need more space and are more exposed to blight. Potatoes are frost-tender in the leaves, responsive to rich soil and moisture, and at their best when lifted carefully, eaten fresh for earlies, or dried and stored cool, dark and frost-free for maincrops.

Sow

Apr

Harvest

Jun – Oct

Depth

Ground planting: trench about 6 in. deep; this is trench depth, not soil cover above the tuber.

Row spacing

Between rows: First and second earlies 24 in.; maincrop 30 in.

Yield (10 ft row)

early varieties: 12 lb; maincrop varieties: 20 lb

Plant spacing

Between plants: Earlies 12 in.; maincrops 16 in.

Ready in

First early 13; second 16–18; maincrop 22 weeks from planting

Recommended varieties
SECOND EARLY
Charlotte

Second-early salad potato with firm yellow flesh, well suited to boiling and serving as new potatoes.

MAINCROP
Maris Piper

Floury maincrop potato for chips, roasting and mash.

MAINCROP
Sarpo Mira

Vigorous maincrop with strong late-blight resistance. Red skin and floury flesh when mature.

FIRST EARLY
Casablanca

First-early potato for an early harvest. Lift young for smaller, tender tubers.

MAINCROP
Desiree

Red-skinned maincrop with pale yellow flesh, useful for everyday cooking.

MAINCROP
Pink Fir Apple

Late salad potato with knobbly tubers and firm, waxy flesh.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 1

Growing & harvesting
Keep developing tubers covered.

Earth or mulch excludes light; do not eat green potatoes.

Choose the crop for your needs.

Earlies give fresh new potatoes; maincrops give larger storage harvests.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile soil improved with compost or well-rotted manure. Potatoes prefer slightly acid soil; avoid liming and rotate the crop.
Avoid frost pockets and waterlogged ground. Newly cleared ground may harbour slugs or wireworms: check before choosing the site.
Looking after the crop
Protect shoots from frost. Earth up or mulch before tubers are exposed; weed carefully and water as tubers swell, especially in pots.
If blight becomes established, remove affected haulm and debris. Where conditions permit, wait about two weeks before lifting; use sound tubers promptly.
Harvesting & storage
Test-lift earlies at a useful size and use fresh. Lift storage crops after haulm dies, before severe frost, forking carefully and collecting every tuber. Flowering alone is not a reliable readiness test. Remove tiny tubers too, to reduce volunteers and disease carry-over.
Dry briefly out of strong light. Store only sound, dry tubers in breathable sacks, cool, dark and frost-free; use sound damaged ones first and discard rot. Use jute, canvas or paper sacks; avoid sealed plastic bags.
Sowing & planting
1 Sprouts upwards

Place seed potatoes at the trench base with sprouts upwards.

2 Cover gently

Cover gently without damaging the sprouts, and water well.

Trench depth Ground planting: trench about 6 in. deep; this is trench depth, not soil cover above the tuber.
Plants Between plants: Earlies 12 in.; maincrops 16 in.
First-early rows 24 in. between rows
Maincrop rows 30 in. between rows

Individual holes are an alternative. For no-dig, shallow-plant under a thick light-excluding mulch. Chitting is most useful for early crops.

Plant earlies in March–April and maincrops in April as local conditions permit. Containers need drainage, ample compost, regular water and continued tuber coverage.

Key risks
BLIGHT

Potato blight spreads rapidly in warm, wet weather, causing brown foliage lesions, collapse and potentially tuber decay.

SLUGS

Slugs tunnel into tubers, particularly in damp soil or beneath covers and mulches.

SCAB

Common scab causes corky skin patches and is favoured by dry conditions as tubers form, particularly in alkaline soil.

EELWORM

Potato cyst nematodes can build up where potatoes are grown repeatedly.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 2

Potato · continued
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
BLIGHT	Brown collapsing foliage; tubers may rot.	Remove affected haulm; allow skins to set before lifting where possible.
SLUGS	Deep tunnels spoil tubers.	Avoid slug refuges; lift mature crops promptly.
SCAB	Corky skin patches on tubers.	Avoid liming; keep soil moist as tubers form.
EELWORM	Stunted patches; cysts on roots.	Rotate; use suitable resistant varieties after diagnosis.
FROST	Young foliage blackens.	Cover shoots before frost; unfrozen plants may regrow.
STORAGE ROTS	Tubers soften or decay in store.	Store only sound dry tubers; inspect and remove rot.
Blackleg	Stem bases blacken; leaves wilt.	Remove affected plants; use healthy certified seed.
Wireworm	Narrow tunnels riddle tubers.	Avoid infested ground; remove larvae and lift promptly.
WART DISEASE	Cauliflower-like growths around eyes.	Do not move soil or tubers; report for official diagnosis.
COLORADO BEETLE	Striped yellow beetles or spotted larvae.	Contain securely, photograph and report; do not release.
Final tips

Check mulch and ridges through the season: exposed tubers green in light and must not be eaten.

Check stored potatoes regularly and remove soft or rotting tubers before decay spreads.

IMPERIAL · 3

Root Crops
Radish.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Summer / Autumn

Radishes are among the fastest root crops and deserve a place for their speed alone: spring sowings can give mild, juicy roots when few other outdoor crops are ready. They are useful in odd corners, window boxes, under protection, or as a quick crop between slower vegetables. The familiar small red and red-white radishes are best eaten young, before heat, age or drought makes them hot, woody, hollow or soft. Winter radishes are a more substantial crop: they include white, pink, black and red-white types, grow for much longer, and can be grated, pickled, braised, stir-fried or stored in cool damp conditions after lifting in autumn.

Mar – Aug

Harvest

Apr – Nov

4–7 days

Salad radishes: 1/2 in.; winter and oriental radishes: about 3/4 in.

6 in. between rows

Yield (10 ft row)

summer varieties: 4 lb; winter varieties: 10 lb

Plant spacing

Between plants: Salad 1–2 in.; winter/Japanese 6–8 in.

Ready in

Salad 3–6; winter 10–12 weeks from sowing

Recommended varieties
SPRING/SUMMER
French Breakfast 3

A familiar long red-and-white summer radish. Sow small batches and pick promptly for crisp, mildly peppery roots.

SPRING/SUMMER
Cherry Belle

A round, bright-red salad radish. A straightforward alternative for rapid crops in beds or containers.

SPRING/SUMMER
Scarlet Globe

A round red summer radish for quick crops and repeat sowings. Harvest young before roots become coarse.

WINTER
China Rose

A pink winter radish for autumn use. Adds a longer-rooted alternative to the round black-skinned storage type.

WINTER
Black Spanish Round

A black-skinned winter radish with firm white flesh. Sow for larger autumn roots rather than treating it as a quick summer radish.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 1

Growing & harvesting
Sun in spring; light shade in summer.

Hot, dry conditions make roots hotter and woodier.

Thin only where needed.

Pull the largest roots first and let smaller ones grow on.

Do not sow winter radishes too early.

They need to grow steadily into autumn, not bolt in summer.

Soil & preparation
Use rich, damp soil with a little compost and a fine tilth for rapid, tender growth.
Choose sun in spring and light shade in summer. Lime acid soil if needed; give winter radishes humus-rich drainage.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow salad radishes

Sow a short drill thinly and cover lightly. Repeat small sowings for succession.

2 Leave room to grow

Leave room between salad radishes; thin crowded seedlings.

Seed depth Salad radishes: 1/2 in.; winter and oriental radishes: about 3/4 in.
Salad rows 6 in. between rows
Winter rows 6 in. between rows
Salad plants Sow or thin to 1-2 in. apart.
Oriental plants Sow or thin to 6-8 in. apart, depending on variety.
Winter plants Sow or thin to 6-8 in. apart, depending on variety.

For a small patch, broadcast seed and rake it in. Winter radishes: sow in July or early August to reduce bolting.

Sow small batches every fortnight. Early sowings can go under cloches, glass or plastic; late-winter sowing is for favourable areas.

After May, cabbage root fly damage is more likely. Summer heat makes rapid growth harder to maintain.

Looking after the crop
Keep rows moist and weed-free. Quick, uninterrupted growth is the secret of crisp, mild radishes; water particularly as roots swell. Dry checks can make roots hot, woody or pithy, so avoid letting young rows dry out between waterings.
Thin only where needed. Pull the largest summer roots first, letting smaller ones grow on, but do not leave any too long.
Protect young leaves from flea beetle with fine mesh or fleece. Clear quick crops promptly for the next crop.
Sow winter radishes at their recommended later dates. Sowing them too early can send plants to seed in summer instead of producing a useful autumn root crop.
Harvesting & storage
Pull spring and summer radishes while small, crisp and mildly flavoured. French Breakfast types are best before they become finger-thick and tough.
Many spring varieties take 40-50 days; very quick crops may be ready in three to four weeks in good conditions. Pull surplus roots rather than leaving them to turn woody or hollow.
Lift winter radishes in October or November before hard frost, or leave hardy kinds in the ground where frost is not severe. Store lifted roots cool and damp, for example in sand.
Key risks
Checked Growth / Poor Root Quality

Turnips, swedes and radishes need steady, quick growth.

FLEA BEETLE

Tiny beetles pepper seedling leaves with holes and can check young crops.

BOLTING

Winter radishes sown before July may flower before forming usable roots.

CABBAGE ROOT FLY

Late and winter radishes are often tunnelled by cabbage root fly maggots, especially after May sowings.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 2

Radish · continued
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
FLEA BEETLE	Shot-holed leaves.	Keep moist; use fine mesh.
BOLTING	Early flowers; poor roots.	Sow winter radishes from July onwards.
CABBAGE ROOT FLY	Roots tunnelled by maggots.	Use mesh; trim minor root damage.
WOODY OR HOLLOW ROOTS	Hot, woody or hollow roots.	Water evenly; thin and harvest promptly.
ACID SOIL	Poor growth in acid soil.	Test soil; lime only where needed.
Slugs and Snails	Chewed seedlings; slime trails.	Check after dark; hand-pick around seedlings.
Final tips

Sow winter radishes in July or early August, not spring.

Clear quick crops promptly for the next crop.

Brassicas
Kale.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Autumn / Winter

Kale, also known as borecole, is a hardy, non-hearting brassica grown for its leaves and young spring shoots. It used to be treated as a plain winter standby, but modern varieties give a wide range of colours, textures and flavours, from deeply curled green leaves to red and flat-leaved types. It is one of the most dependable crops for autumn, winter and early spring, often standing when little else is available, and the flavour is generally better after frost.

Mar – Jun

Harvest

Sep – Apr

Germination

7–12 days

Depth

about 1/2 in.

Row spacing

6 in. between seed rows

Yield per plant

2 lb

Plant spacing

About 18 in. between standard plants; allow more room for large varieties. Follow the packet for compact or baby-leaf crops.

Ready in

First picking depends on variety and leaf size; main crops give autumn/winter leaves and later spring shoots.

Recommended varieties
MODERN AND COLOURED
Nero di Toscana

A dark, strap-leaved kale for repeated picking. Its textured leaves are especially useful in soups, stews and winter cooking.

CURLY-LEAVED
Reflex F1

A green curly kale for productive winter picking. A useful maincrop choice where familiar curled leaves are preferred.

MODERN AND COLOURED
Red Russian

A flat-leaved kale with purple stems and tender young leaves. Useful for salads when young and cooking when larger.

MODERN AND COLOURED
Redbor F1

A purple-red curly kale that adds colour to the plot. Pick regularly for tender leaves and continued growth.

MODERN AND COLOURED
Yurok F1

A dark-leaved kale in the Tuscan style. Retain as a modern alternative where this leaf shape is preferred.

Key risks
Cabbage Caterpillars

Caterpillars of cabbage white butterfly, cabbage moth and related pests chew holes in leaves.

Club Root (Finger and Toe)

Swollen, distorted roots cause poor growth and wilting in sunshine.

Cabbage Whitefly

Small white-winged insects and scale-like young live below brassica leaves; adults fly up when disturbed.

Mealy Aphid

Large clusters of waxy, greyish 'greenflies' occur on the underside of leaves and tips of plants from June onwards in hot, dry weather.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 1

Growing & harvesting
Fertile, settled soil

Drain well; firm transplants.

Keep plants steady

Water; prevent wind rock.

Spring feeding

Feed only weak spring growth.

Soil & preparation
Choose sun or light shade and well-drained soil. Kale tolerates many soils but yields best in fertile ground.
Follow early crops; weed and add mature compost as needed. Use settled or no-dig soil. Firm transplants without compacting wet ground; lime only if a soil test indicates a need.
Sowing & planting
1 Raise young plants

Sow thinly in a seed bed or modules; cover and thin seedlings.

2 Set deeper and firm

Set lowest leaves just above soil; firm well and water in.

Final rows Usually 18–24 in. apart for full-size plants; adjust for variety and method.
Transplant height 4-6 in.

Rape kale: sow direct and thin in stages.

Water nursery rows before lifting. After early crops, sow June–early July; transplant promptly when ready, often July–early August. Allow establishment time and protect all crops from pests.

Looking after the crop
Weed carefully and water young plants. Check and secure loose stems after windy weather, without treading heavily on wet soil.
Remove yellow leaves, earth up in autumn and stake tall plants on exposed sites.
Support insect-proof mesh where needed and secure bird protection. Keep covers clear of leaves and check beneath them; leaf colour gives no immunity.
Give an organic liquid feed only if spring growth is weak.
Harvesting & storage
Pick tender outer leaves little and often. Leave the growing top and enough foliage for repeat crops; reject tough or yellow leaves.
Pick young, tender side shoots in late winter and spring, usually about 4–5 in. long; timing varies with variety and weather. Removing a mature crown encourages shoots; this is a separate method, not routine leaf picking.
Pick Red Russian leaves young; baby-leaf harvest is not limited to spring. Chop healthy finished stems into short 4–6 in. pieces to help them compost; follow disease guidance for affected roots.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Cabbage Caterpillars	Holes; feeding caterpillars.	Hand-pick eggs and larvae; use fine mesh.
Club Root (Finger and Toe)	Swollen roots; wilting.	Avoid infected soil; clean tools. Test before liming; no cure.
Cabbage Whitefly	White flies under leaves.	Tolerate minor colonies; encourage natural enemies.
Mealy Aphid	Grey colonies; curled leaves.	Squash damaging colonies; encourage predators.
Pigeons	Pecked or stripped leaves.	Net securely, clear of leaves.
Slugs and Snails	Holes; seedlings eaten.	Hand-pick at dusk; clear yellow leaves near seedlings.
Cabbage Root Fly	Wilting; tunnelled roots.	Use collars or mesh on a rotated bed.
Flea Beetle	Tiny holes; jumping beetles.	Mesh young plants; keep growth steady.
Final tips

Match spacing to variety and method; give larger plants more room.

Winter-worn plants may still provide tender spring shoots.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 2

Salads & Leaves
Beet, Leaf.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Leaf beets are a useful answer for gardeners who like spinach but find true spinach quick to bolt or difficult in dry weather. Swiss chard, seakale beet, spinach beet and perpetual spinach are all grown for leaves rather than swollen roots, and a few plants can provide many pickings over a long season. Swiss chard has broad leaves with thick, edible midribs, often white but sometimes red, yellow or pink, and it is ornamental enough for the flower border. Spinach beet has a plainer green leaf, is used much like spinach in the kitchen. The main rule is to pick regularly: small leaves are tender and useful for salads or cooking, while over-large leaves become tougher and the plant slows down. In mild winters established plants may survive to give another flush of leaves in early spring before they send up flowering stems.

Recommended varieties
Bright Lights

A colourful chard selection with stems in several shades. Harvest young leaves for salads or larger leaves and stems for cooking.

Rhubarb Chard

Red stalks and dark leaves make this chard decorative as well as useful. Treat it as a red-stemmed type unless a cultivar is specified.

Spinach Beet

A leaf beet grown for repeated picking of green leaves. Useful as a cooking green through a longer season than true spinach.

Fordhook Giant

A white-stemmed chard with broad green leaves. A useful kitchen choice when leaf yield matters more than mixed stem colours.

Key risks
Slugs

Leaf beet is usually hardy and trouble-free, but slugs may nibble young plants, especially in autumn or damp weather.

Manganese Deficiency

Yellowing between leaf veins can indicate a nutrient problem, but symptoms overlap.

Leaf Spot

Leaf spots may have pale brown centres and dark brown or purple margins, roughly 1/4 in. across.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 1

Growing & harvesting
Keep leaves growing steadily.

Rich soil, regular picking and reliable moisture give tender leaves.

Choose the type for your kitchen.

Chard gives colourful stems; spinach beet is grown mainly for its leaves.

Soil & preparation
Grow in fertile soil with compost or well-rotted manure, avoiding waterlogged ground. Check pH before liming; about 6.5 suits the crop.
Chard tolerates a wide range of conditions, while spinach beet prefers cool, moist weather and a deep, fertile soil.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow seed clusters

Sow the corky seed clusters in rows. Several seedlings may emerge from each cluster.

2 Thin young plants

Thin once seedlings are established and large enough to handle. Keep the strongest plants and allow room for the chosen type.

Seed depth 1 in.
Rows 18 in. between rows
Final plants Between plants: 12 in. for mature leaves; 2 in. for baby leaves

Each corky seed cluster can produce several seedlings: thin to the strongest. Pre-soaking is optional.

Sow spinach beet in spring and again in midsummer for a longer supply. Give chard more room when growing it for stems; late-summer sowings can overwinter in mild areas.

Looking after the crop
Thin for mature leaves or baby-leaf picking, weed regularly and cut off early flower stems to prolong cropping. Leave the strongest seedlings. Keep the ground clean while plants establish so that weeds do not compete with the young crop.
Water in dry spells and mulch to conserve moisture. Regular picking encourages fresh, tender leaves. Steady moisture maintains picking quality and keeps new leaves tender.
Harvesting & storage
Pick outer leaves without disturbing the roots, leaving the young centre to keep growing. Twist or pull each outer leaf downwards gently. Do not strip a plant bare: its central leaves must continue feeding the plant.
Use small leaves in salads; cook larger leaves and thick chard midribs separately if needed. Chard midribs take longer to cook than the leaf blades, so start them first. Larger leaves are edible but tougher than young salad leaves.
Overwintered plants can give an early spring picking before they flower. In a mild winter this second flush may last a month or two before flowering stems appear.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Slugs	Young leaves and seedlings are chewed.	Check young plants after dark; hand-pick and protect establishment.
Manganese Deficiency	Yellowing between veins; margins may curl.	Check drainage and soil pH; avoid over-liming and confirm the cause.
Leaf Spot	Brown-centred spots with darker borders.	Remove affected leaves and debris; rotate and avoid crowding.
Final tips

Pick a little from several plants to keep a supply of young leaves coming.

Keep late sowings growing before winter; they may provide useful early spring leaves.

IMPERIAL · 2

Stalks & Shoots
Celery.
DIFFICULTY
Difficult
5/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Autumn / Winter

Celery is a moisture-loving crop grown for crisp, strongly flavoured stems, and it is much easier to enjoy than to grow beautifully. Traditional trench celery is grown for winter flavour, but it demands deep preparation, regular watering and careful earthing-up to exclude light from the stems. Self-blanching celery is simpler because close planting and a dense canopy do much of the blanching work, although it is less hardy and usually best harvested before cold weather. Celery leaf is a useful lighter option, giving repeated pickings of smaller stems. Whichever type you grow, the essentials are humus-rich soil, steady surface moisture and clean, weed-free ground; dry checks lead to bitterness, stringiness and bolting, while slugs often spoil the look of the crop even when the flavour remains good.

SELF BLANCHING
Victoria F1

Self-blanching celery with crisp, pale stalks. An easier choice than traditional trench varieties.

SELF BLANCHING
Golden Self-Blanching

Traditional self-blanching celery with pale stems. Water regularly to keep stalks tender.

SELF BLANCHING

Red-stemmed trench celery with a strong flavour. Needs blanching and winter protection.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 1

Growing & harvesting
Rich soil and steady moisture.

Plenty of compost or manure helps on drier ground.

Do not let celery dry out.

Prepare traditional trenches as follows: Trench types: 12 in. deep, 18 in. wide; refill with soil and compost to 4 in. below ground.

1 Raise seedlings

Surface sow in March–April, or cover very lightly. Keep warm, damp and ventilated. Pot on when large enough to handle and harden off gradually.

2 Plant a block

After frost risk, plant self-blanching or green types in a close block at module depth. Water regularly to keep growth moving.

Looking after the crop
Keep celery evenly moist throughout growth. Water thoroughly whenever needed, especially in hot weather; do not let the root zone dry out. Dry checks make stems tough and stringy.

Cut self-blanching celery before the first frost and before stems toughen. Cutting above soil may give a small second picking in mild weather.
Pick larger outside stems of celery leaf regularly to encourage new growth.
Harvest trench celery in late autumn and early winter. Protect in severe frost and replace soil around plants left in the row.
Lift from one row end, replacing soil around remaining plants. Keep harvested stalks cool and use promptly.

Potatoes can feed a household from a small plot, with dense foliage useful on newly prepared ground; check former grassland for wireworms first. Growing & harvesting
Keep developing tubers covered.

Choose the crop for your needs.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile soil improved with compost or well-rotted manure. Potatoes prefer slightly acid soil; avoid liming and rotate the crop.
Avoid frost pockets and waterlogged ground. Newly cleared ground may harbour slugs or wireworms: check before choosing the site.
Looking after the crop

Celery is a moisture-loving crop grown for crisp, strongly flavoured stems, and it is much easier to enjoy than to grow beautifully. Traditional trench celery is grown for winter flavour, but it demands deep preparation, regular watering and careful earthing-up to exclude light from the stems. Beetroot is much more than a boiled-and-pickled salad extra. Grown well, it has a sweet, earthy flavour, can be eaten raw in grated winter salads, cooked as a hot vegetable, used for borsch and chutneys, and even harvested for its young leaves. It is a cool-climate root crop that likes well-drained, humus-rich soil, steady moisture and no check to growth. It starts slowly, but once seedlings are established the roots swell quickly, especially if they are grown in short, repeated sowings or in module-raised clumps. Beetroot transplants better than many root crops, so early sowings under cover can give golf-ball-sized roots by late spring, while later sowings provide summer, autumn and storage roots. The best roots are lifted before they become large, woody or leathery; in mild winters some can remain in the ground, but severe frost can freeze them through and lead to rotting.

Cauliflower is one of the most rewarding brassicas, but also one of the least forgiving. The curd is a tight mass of flower buds, and the plant has to make strong, uninterrupted growth before it will produce a worthwhile head. Poor soil, loose planting, drought, overcrowding or a check after transplanting can all lead to tiny button heads or blind plants. Once a curd has formed it must be watched closely and cut before the surface loosens or the flower buds begin to open.

Broad beans are among the most dependable and useful garden crops. They are hardier than peas, will tolerate heavier soils than many beans, and can give fresh pods at a time when there is still relatively little else to pick. Choose sunny, moisture-retentive but free-draining ground where beans did not grow last year. Avoid waterlogging; lime very acid soil towards pH 6.5.
Ground enriched for a previous crop is ideal. Add compost or well-rotted manure in autumn if soil is poor.

1 Sow large beans

Sow into prepared soil. Add spare seeds at row ends to provide seedlings for gaps.

2 Establish a double row

Runner beans are the classic British summer bean: vigorous, ornamental climbers with red, white, pink or bicoloured flowers and long flat pods that can crop heavily from late summer into autumn. They are less drought-tolerant than French beans and need a rich, moisture-retentive root run, so they flourish in moist, mild summers and struggle in hot, dry spells unless watered well. Choose a sunny site with moist, free-draining ground.

Pinch out at support height.

Remove growing points once plants reach the tops of their supports.

Keep roots steadily moist.

Water thoroughly from flowering onwards for a good pod set.

Soil & preparation
Use sunny, sheltered, rich ground that holds moisture but drains well. Lime acid soil if needed towards pH 6.5.
Prepare deeply with compost or well-rotted manure in autumn or winter. Avoid shading neighbouring crops.

1 Set sturdy supports

Install crossed poles in a double line and tie a horizontal bar along the top. Wigwams, netting or strings are alternatives.

2 Sow beside the poles

Sow at the base of the supports once frost risk has passed and the soil is warm. Sow spare seeds to fill gaps.

3 Establish the double row

Tie young stems loosely to the supports until they climb naturally. Protect seedlings from slugs.

Protect young plants from slugs and tie them loosely to supports until they climb naturally. Hoe while young, then mulch once growth is strong. Mulch is particularly useful on light soils and in dry gardens, where roots dry out quickly.

Endive is a cool-season salad plant with more flavour and bitterness than lettuce, though less of lettuce's crispness. It can be eaten raw in mixed salads or cooked, and both curly-leaved frisée types and broader-leaved Batavian or escarole types are useful. Pick individual leaves or whole plants according to the crop. Cut Chinese cabbage once hearts form, before damaging frost.
Mizuna and hardy mustards can give protected winter pickings. Leaf radish quality declines as winter approaches unless protected.

Growing & harvesting
Keep roots warm and evenly moist.

Cold, wet compost checks young plants; avoid both drought and waterlogging.

Check the variety’s flower instructions.

Soil & preparation
Use rich, moisture-retentive but free-draining compost in pots, bags or an enriched bed. Fresh compost is useful where border soil is suspect.
Provide warm, humid air with ventilation. Avoid stagnant conditions and cold, sodden roots.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow on edge

Sow one seed edgeways in a warm pot or module. Water as compost starts drying; avoid keeping small pots constantly wet.

2 Handle gently

Plant in settled, warm greenhouse conditions. Protect the fragile roots and stem; use a pot, growbag or prepared mound and water in.

Pots / bags / mounds 1 per pot at least 12 in. wide/deep; 2 per growbag; 2 ft between mounds

Looking after the crop
Train on a string or cane; stop or turn the leader at the roof and prune laterals to suit the variety. Keep the plant from becoming a dense tangle. Depending on the variety, one or two upper side shoots can trail down after the leader reaches its support.

Use fertile, well-drained border soil enriched with compost, or suitable pots and growing bags with fresh peat-free compost.

Keep moisture even, especially once bulbs begin swelling. Drought checks reduce juiciness and encourage bolting. A surface dressing of compost is useful on light ground or after an earlier crop has used much of the fertility.
Hoe or hand-weed while plants are young: small plants compete poorly with weeds.
Thin direct-sown rows promptly. Crowded plants make smaller, less well-shaped bulbs and may run up to stem.
Earth up lightly where useful to keep the base tender and moist, without covering the growing centre or trapping rot around old sheaths.
Harvesting & storage
Cut bulbs at a useful size before they become fibrous or frosted. If a small bulb starts elongating, harvest promptly; it is unlikely to fatten. Baby bulbs can be taken at about 2 in. across; full bulbs are commonly cut at about 4–6 in. while still tender.
Trim tough stems and use fronds for flavouring. Lift before hard frost; keep sound autumn bulbs cool and frost-free for short-term use.
If lower sheaths rot, lift promptly, discard rotten tissue and use only firm sound parts; discard extensively rotted bulbs.

The first flush of mushrooms is an exciting reward for careful indoor growing. This page covers cultivated button and chestnut mushrooms (Agaricus bisporus), grown in prepared mushroom compost. Fresh ready-spawned kits give the simplest start for small quantities; preparing mushroom compost from raw ingredients requires controlled composting and conditioning. Growing & harvesting
Start with prepared mushroom compost.

A fresh ready-spawned kit is the simplest route for small quantities.

Soil & preparation
Cultivated button mushrooms need specially prepared mushroom compost, not ordinary garden soil. Buy fresh spawned compost or a kit. Commercial compost commonly uses straw, manure and gypsum, processed before spawning.
Making mushroom compost involves both initial composting and a controlled pasteurisation and conditioning stage to remove ammonia. Appearance or a fixed number of turnings alone cannot establish that it is ready. Use a complete tested method and suitable equipment.
Button mushrooms use a moist casing layer after the compost is colonised. Use the kit’s supplied or recommended casing and timing; not every mushroom species needs casing. Keep it moist without saturation.
Establishing the crop
1 Start with spawned compost

For the straightforward indoor route, buy fresh ready-spawned compost in a bag, bucket or box. Keep it shaded from direct sunlight.

2 Maintain moisture

Once casing is added, keep it moist but not wet. Water lightly when needed and avoid saturation. This illustrates the supplied-compost route.

Looking after the crop
Temperatures differ between spawn growth and cropping. Follow the button-mushroom kit’s instructions for each stage and keep conditions steady, with ventilation and no direct sun.
The compost can generate its own heat while the mycelium spreads. Avoid overheating and follow the supplier’s temperature range; a single upper temperature limit is not reliable for every strain or kit.
Cropping around 61–64°F suits many button-mushroom kits, but follow the supplier’s range. Keep the casing lightly moist with careful watering, never saturated.
Harvesting & storage
Pick button mushrooms at the size you prefer, before the veil opens for closed buttons or later for open caps. Crops arrive in flushes with rests between them; the start and duration depend on the kit and growing conditions.
For cultivated button mushrooms, twist gently to lift the mushroom with minimal disturbance. Trim off dirty stem bases and remove broken remnants; refill holes with suitable casing where the kit recommends it.
After the final crop, compost healthy spent substrate or use it as a soil improver. Mushroom compost can contain substantial soluble salts, so weather it before use near seedlings or salt-sensitive plants. Start new crops with fresh prepared material.
Between flushes, maintain the kit’s recommended moisture with clean water and wait for the next crop. Once exhausted, remove old substrate, wash and rinse reusable containers, and let them dry before starting again.

Beetroot is much more than a boiled-and-pickled salad extra. Grown well, it has a sweet, earthy flavour, can be eaten raw in grated winter salads, cooked as a hot vegetable, used for borsch and chutneys, and even harvested for its young leaves. It is a cool-climate root crop that likes well-drained, humus-rich soil, steady moisture and no check to growth. Beetroot transplants better than many root crops, so early sowings under cover can give golf-ball-sized roots by late spring, while later sowings provide summer, autumn and storage roots. Cauliflower is one of the most rewarding brassicas, but also one of the least forgiving. Protect seedlings from slugs; keep beds clean and weed-free, especially below low dwarf pods.
Dwarf varieties normally need no support. Give climbers canes, netting, wigwams or strings early; guide wandering shoots onto them.

Water and use an organic liquid feed after the first flush of pods to encourage a smaller second crop.

Pick tender green pods every few days before the beans inside swell. Search carefully for pods hidden in climbing foliage.

For dried haricots, let pods ripen and turn straw-coloured. Finish drying plants in an airy shed if needed, then shell and dry beans fully before storing airtight. Hang plants upside down under cover so air can circulate around the ripening pods.

French beans may drop flowers or set few pods when roots are dry, especially in hot weather.

Birds can be a nuisance in several ways.

Runner beans are the classic British summer bean: vigorous, ornamental climbers with red, white, pink or bicoloured flowers and long flat pods that can crop heavily from late summer into autumn. Fruits may be oval, round or long, and varieties range from the familiar dark purple to white, violet and striped forms.

Capsicums include both sweet peppers and chillies: colourful, heat-loving members of the tomato and potato family. In their native climate they are perennial plants, but in Britain they are grown as tender annuals and are most reliable under glass or in a warm, sheltered position. Green peppers are edible but are still an immature stage; if left to ripen they change colour and, in many varieties, become sweeter or hotter and more deeply flavoured. The crop is therefore a balance between earlier, heavier green harvests and later, smaller harvests of fully coloured fruit.

Growing & harvesting
Keep roots warm and evenly moist.

Cold, wet compost checks young plants; avoid both drought and waterlogging.

Check the variety’s flower instructions.

Greenhouse types grown without pollination need any male flowers removed.

Soil & preparation
Use rich, moisture-retentive but free-draining compost in pots, bags or an enriched bed. Fresh compost is useful where border soil is suspect.
Provide warm, humid air with ventilation. Avoid stagnant conditions and cold, sodden roots.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow on edge

Sow one seed edgeways in a warm pot or module. Water as compost starts drying; avoid keeping small pots constantly wet.

2 Handle gently

Plant in settled, warm greenhouse conditions. Protect the fragile roots and stem; use a pot, growbag or prepared mound and water in.

Seed depth 1–2 cm
Pots / bags / mounds 1 per pot at least 30 cm wide/deep; 2 per growbag; 60 cm between mounds
Mound method only prepared greenhouse mounds about 15 cm deep and 30 cm wide, if using the mound method

Looking after the crop
Train on a string or cane; stop or turn the leader at the roof and prune laterals to suit the variety. Keep the plant from becoming a dense tangle. Depending on the variety, one or two upper side shoots can trail down after the leader reaches its support.
Water steadily and shade in intense heat. Dampen paths for humidity without soaking roots; ventilate to limit mould.
Remove male flowers where the variety requires unpollinated fruit, including any appearing on all-female types. Give regular organic liquid feed once fruits swell. Check the seed packet: varieties that require pollination must retain their male flowers.
Harvesting & storage
Cut fruits at a useful size before they yellow or become tough and seedy. Frequent picking keeps plants cropping. Cut rather than pull fruit from the vine. Mature fruit left to ripen can slow or stop the production of new flowers and cucumbers.
Inspect daily in hot weather. Discard unusually bitter fruit; cooking or trimming is not a reliable remedy.

Allow ample room for trailing stems. Pumpkin stems can root into bare, moist soil; smaller varieties suit shorter seasons.
Sowing & planting
1 Start in a pot

Sow singly under cover in small pots or modules. Pot on if roots fill the container, then harden off gradually. Direct-sow after frost into warm soil.

2 Give room to spread

Set one plant in each compost-rich station. Give pumpkins ample room to trail and root at the stem nodes.

Seed depth by route Indoors: squash 1.5 cm, pumpkins 1 cm; outdoors: 2.5 cm
Spacing by type Bush squash: 90 cm each way; trailing squash and ordinary pumpkins: about 1.5 m; giant pumpkins: 2 m or more, following the variety’s instructions
Final plants one plant per station

Winter squash needs the whole season: start indoors in April or direct-sow only into warm late-spring soil. Summer squash can start in May–early June. Remove protective fleece as plants establish and begin flowering.

Looking after the crop
Water well at planting and in dry spells; mulch with compost and remove weeds before the foliage spreads. Large leaves shade the soil but do not remove the need for watering while fruit swells. Clear weeds before their seeds fall beneath the canopy.
Allow insect access to flowers and hand-pollinate if necessary. For giant pumpkins, restrict fruit numbers; support developing fruit above wet soil. Ordinary eating varieties can carry several fruits on strong plants; the one-fruit approach is for giant show pumpkins. Tiles or boards can keep fruit off persistently wet soil.
Harvesting & storage
Pick summer squash young and tender. Leave winter squash to harden and develop corky stalks, then cut before frost.
Leave about 10 cm of sound stalk. Cure ripe fruit in sunshine for 1–2 weeks, then store dry and airy at 10–15°C. Use sound unripe fruit promptly. Bring curing fruit under cover if frost or rain threatens. Keep stored fruit apart and inspect regularly for soft patches. Never carry a squash by its stalk: a break allows rot to enter.
Discard unusually bitter or rotten fruit. Keep pumpkins intended for eating separate from carved outdoor displays.
Key risks
SLUGS

Slugs attack seedlings and young plants, especially in cold wet conditions, and may damage fruit resting on the soil.

MILDEW

Powdery mildew produces a white coating on leaves, often late in the season.

STEM DAMAGE AND ROT

A broken stalk or damaged skin provides an entry point for storage rot.

No Fruit

Poor pollination can leave flowers without developing fruit, especially in cool weather.

Growing & harvesting
Plant full-sized corn in a block.

Pollen must reach the silks. Baby corn is picked before pollination and can grow in rows.

Keep plants warm and well watered.

Moisture matters especially during flowering and cob filling.

Soil & preparation
Use deep, fertile, humus-rich soil that holds moisture without becoming cold and waterlogged. Work in well-rotted compost before planting.
Choose a sunny, sheltered, warm site. Neutral to slightly acid soil suits the crop; warmth and drainage are vital in cooler areas.
Looking after the crop
Weed while plants are small, avoiding the spreading roots. Mulch and water during dry weather, particularly as tassels shed pollen and cobs swell.

Harvesting & storage
Test a cob when silks brown: a pierced kernel should release milky juice. Clear watery juice is early; doughy contents mean it is past its best. Test frequently as the silks brown: the best stage passes quickly. Kernel colour varies by variety and is not a reliable ripeness test on its own.
Twist cobs off carefully and use promptly. Check for smaller second cobs; pick baby corn while young, with silks still white.
Sowing & planting
1 Raise and plant

Sow in warm pots or modules; thin to one. Harden off, then plant the intact rootball in warm weather and water in.

2 Block for full cobs

BLIGHT

Greenhouse Whitefly

GROWING GUIDES
METRIC · 1

Growing & harvesting
Water steadily and ventilate.

Even root moisture and moving air help fruit develop without splits or mould.

Train to the variety’s habit.

Remove side shoots from cordons; bush types need a different routine.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile, well-drained border soil enriched with compost, or suitable pots and growing bags with fresh peat-free compost.
Avoid waterlogging and stale humid air. Containers need closer watering and feeding attention than a well-prepared border.
Looking after the crop
Tie cordons loosely, remove young side shoots and take off yellow lower leaves sparingly. Stop two leaves above the final truss at the chosen height or near season’s end. Retain healthy foliage to feed and shade fruit. Follow separate pruning instructions for bush and semi-determinate varieties.
Water roots steadily and feed organically at the product’s rate as fruit develops. Ventilate in heat, tap flowering trusses gently and adjust autumn watering to growth. Dry-to-wet swings encourage splitting and blossom-end rot.
Harvesting & storage
Pick fully coloured fruit gently and use promptly. Bring sound unripe fruit indoors before cold ends the crop; check ripening trays and discard decay. Ripen at room temperature; a ripe apple or banana nearby can help.
Sowing & planting
1 Grow on in a pot

Sow in trays or small pots, keeping compost moist but not wet. Prick out and pot on as needed; keep seedlings bright for stout stems.

2 Plant and support

Plant well-rooted plants into pots, growbags or a soil bed once the greenhouse is warm. Water first, set slightly deeper and support cordons with a cane or string.

Pots / growbags One plant per 30–45 cm diameter pot; two per standard growbag. Use peat-free potting compost.
Pot spacing For upright cordons, allow about 60 cm between pot centres so foliage has room.
Soil beds 45–60 cm between plants in compost-enriched soil; use the wider spacing for vigorous cordons and airflow.

For unheated cover, sow around March in gentle warmth near 20°C. Earlier heated-house crops need reliable warmth and bright light through winter.

Growing & harvesting
Choose a suitable outdoor variety.

Early cropping and a warm, sheltered site improve the chance of ripe fruit.

Keep watering even.

Dry-to-wet swings split fruit and can encourage blossom-end rot.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile, well-drained soil enriched with mature compost in a sunny, sheltered spot. Improve heavy clay well before planting.
Pots and growing bags suit patios or limited space, but need frequent watering and regular organic feeding.
Sowing & planting
1 Grow on and harden

Raise seedlings under cover in spring or buy sturdy pot-grown plants. Harden them off gradually before outdoor planting.

2 Plant beside support

Plant after frost risk in settled warm weather. Water first, preserve the rootball and set slightly deeper. Support tall types and tie in regularly.

Tall plants Between plants: 45–60 cm, allowing more room for vigorous plants

Support and side-shoot cordons; remove yellow leaves sparingly. Stop above the final useful truss by late summer. Bush types normally need no side-shooting or stopping. Allow room for a large perennial.

Choose a sunny, sheltered site with rich, moist but well-drained soil. Improve heavy clay and avoid winter waterlogging.

1 Position the offset

2 Firm at the same level

Growing & harvesting
Good drainage is essential.

Choose a sunny, sheltered site and enrich the soil with compost or well-rotted manure.

Soil & preparation
Choose sunny, sheltered, well-drained ground. Add compost or well-rotted manure; lime very acid soil if needed. Improve drainage or use a raised bed on heavy ground.
Clear perennial weeds before planting: their roots are difficult to remove once tangled with the crowns.
Sowing & planting
1 Prepare a mound

Prepare clean, well-drained ground and a low mound of fine soil in the trench. Keep bought crowns moist until planting.

2 Spread the roots

3 Cover the roots

Wait two years after planting crowns, or three years from seed. Let uncut spears form fern to build strong roots.
Cut finger-thick spears by 18 cm tall, about 2.5 cm below soil level. Pick regularly before spears turn woody. Use a sharp knife and avoid adjacent emerging shoots. Check every few days in cool weather and daily in warm spells.
Cut for six weeks in the first harvest year, then up to eight weeks. Stop by mid-June, sooner if weak, and let later spears form fern.

Florence fennel, or bulb fennel, is a sweet, aniseed-flavoured umbellifer grown for the swollen bases of its leaf-stalks. It belongs to the same broad family as carrot, parsnip and celeriac, but is eaten quite differently: sliced raw in salads, cooked gently for a soft creamy flavour, or used in soups and ratatouille. The feathery leaves are also edible, with a gentle aniseed flavour. Modern varieties have made it easier to grow by reducing the tendency to bolt before useful bulbs form. Match the variety to its sowing season and keep young plants growing steadily: drought, crowding or root checks can give stemmy plants instead of juicy bulbs. Summer sowings after an early crop are useful for autumn harvesting. Harvest while the bulbs are tender, before they become fibrous, stemmy or frosted.

Growing & harvesting
Keep growth steady and moist.

Drought, crowding and root disturbance can spoil bulb development.

Match sowing time to the variety.

Summer sowings usually give more reliable UK autumn bulbs.

Soil & preparation
Choose deep, fertile, moisture-retentive soil. Good humus levels help produce tender, juicy bulbs rather than small, dry ones.
Prepare the ground before sowing or planting with well-rotted manure or compost. Avoid waterlogging.
A compost dressing about 5 cm deep, spread well before planting, feeds the crop and helps hold summer moisture.
Sowing & planting
1 Raise in modules

Sow in modules under cover from May, or outdoors in June–July. Keep young plants warm and growing steadily.

2 Plant level

Plant while seedlings are still growing strongly. Keep the rootball intact, set at module depth without burying the growing point, and water well.

Rows 30 cm between rows
Direct-sown plants Between plants: 30 cm for full bulbs; 15 cm for baby bulbs

June and July sowings are useful after spring cabbage, spinach or salads. Earlier sowing needs a suitable variety and protected conditions; avoid leaving module plants to become checked.

Looking after the crop
Keep moisture even, especially once bulbs begin swelling. Drought checks reduce juiciness and encourage bolting. A surface dressing of compost is useful on light ground or after an earlier crop has used much of the fertility.
Hoe or hand-weed while plants are young: small plants compete poorly with weeds.
Thin direct-sown rows promptly. Crowded plants make smaller, less well-shaped bulbs and may run up to stem.
Earth up lightly where useful to keep the base tender and moist, without covering the growing centre or trapping rot around old sheaths.
Harvesting & storage
Cut bulbs at a useful size before they become fibrous or frosted. If a small bulb starts elongating, harvest promptly; it is unlikely to fatten. Baby bulbs can be taken at about 5 cm across; full bulbs are commonly cut at about 10–15 cm while still tender.
Trim tough stems and use fronds for flavouring. Lift before hard frost; keep sound autumn bulbs cool and frost-free for short-term use.
If lower sheaths rot, lift promptly, discard rotten tissue and use only firm sound parts; discard extensively rotted bulbs.

Rhubarb is grown like a long-lived perennial vegetable, although it is usually cooked and eaten as a fruit. It produces tart spring stems, coloured green to red according to variety from large crowns, and the leaves are not eaten. Rhubarb suits cool climates and benefits from winter dormancy. Green-stemmed varieties are edible too: stem colour is not a ripeness test. Once established in a moist, well-drained, compost-rich corner, a crown can crop for many years with little attention beyond feeding, mulching, watering in dry springs and removing flower stems.

METRIC · 1

Growing & harvesting
Let young crowns build strength.

Leave the first year unpicked and take only a light crop in the second.

Eat the stalks, never the leaves.

Twist stalks away cleanly and leave plenty of foliage to feed the crown.

Soil & preparation
Choose a permanent, open position with rich, moist but well-drained soil. Avoid winter waterlogging and clear perennial weeds.
Prepare with compost, leaf mould or rotted manure. Rhubarb tolerates slightly acid soil; do not lime routinely. Allow space for vigorous roots at a plot edge.
Sowing & planting
1 Set the crown

Use a bought crown or a vigorous piece divided during winter dormancy. Set it right way up, with buds or new shoots just above the soil.

2 Firm and water

Firm the soil around the crown and water in. Do not bury new shoots; leave room for a substantial permanent clump.

Rows 90 cm between rows
Crowns 90 cm between plants

Seed is an alternative: grow young plants on for late-summer or autumn planting. Crowns preserve named varieties and crop sooner.

Looking after the crop
Mulch annually with compost or well-rotted manure, keeping the central crown clear.
Water during dry spells, especially in spring: dry soil gives shorter, thinner and more stringy stalks.
Remove flower stalks promptly when they appear, rather than letting the plant divert energy away from useful leaves and stems.
Force a strong established crown in late winter with a light-proof pot. Check for slugs; remove the cover after picking and rest it for the season. Do not force the same crown in consecutive years.
Harvesting & storage
Leave new crowns unpicked in year one; take a light second-year crop. At each picking leave at least two-thirds of the stems and all thin ones.
Mature plants crop in spring and early summer; stop the usual harvest by late June so leaves rebuild the crown.
Grip near the base, twist and pull gently; avoid cut stumps. Remove and compost the poisonous leaf; eat only the stalk.
Key risks
CROWN ROT

Decay at the crown can cause weak, dull stems and rotting buds.

SLUGS UNDER FORCING POTS

Slugs may hide inside forcing pots or buckets and damage the tender forced stems.

POOR GROWTH OR STRINGY STEMS

Usually linked to dry soil, lack of organic matter, overcropping, or forcing the same crown too often.

HONEY FUNGUS

Honey fungus can cause rhubarb crowns to decline and die.

The first flush of mushrooms is an exciting reward for careful indoor growing. This page covers cultivated button and chestnut mushrooms (Agaricus bisporus), grown in prepared mushroom compost. They need shelter from direct sunlight and can crop while outdoor vegetable beds are quiet. Fresh ready-spawned kits give the simplest start for small quantities; preparing mushroom compost from raw ingredients requires controlled composting and conditioning. Follow the supplier’s instructions for each stage. Other edible mushroom species need different substrates and growing conditions. For the simplest route, buy a fresh ready-spawned button-mushroom kit in a bag, bucket or box. Check the supplier’s start-by date and begin promptly; pre-started kits may already have completed much of the colonisation stage. Button mushrooms use a moist casing layer after the compost is colonised. Use the kit’s supplied or recommended casing and timing; not every mushroom species needs casing. Keep it moist without saturation. Pick button mushrooms at the size you prefer, before the veil opens for closed buttons or later for open caps. Crops arrive in flushes with rests between them; the start and duration depend on the kit and growing conditions.

GROWING GUIDES
METRIC · 1

Growing & harvesting
Start with prepared mushroom compost.

A fresh ready-spawned kit is the simplest route for small quantities.

Keep conditions steady.

Avoid direct sun, temperature extremes and waterlogged casing.

Soil & preparation
Cultivated button mushrooms need specially prepared mushroom compost, not ordinary garden soil. Buy fresh spawned compost or a kit. Commercial compost commonly uses straw, manure and gypsum, processed before spawning.
Making mushroom compost involves both initial composting and a controlled pasteurisation and conditioning stage to remove ammonia. Appearance or a fixed number of turnings alone cannot establish that it is ready. Use a complete tested method and suitable equipment.
Button mushrooms use a moist casing layer after the compost is colonised. Use the kit’s supplied or recommended casing and timing; not every mushroom species needs casing. Keep it moist without saturation.
Establishing the crop
1 Start with spawned compost

For the straightforward indoor route, buy fresh ready-spawned compost in a bag, bucket or box. Keep it shaded from direct sunlight.

2 Maintain moisture

Once casing is added, keep it moist but not wet. Water lightly when needed and avoid saturation. This illustrates the supplied-compost route.

Looking after the crop
Temperatures differ between spawn growth and cropping. Follow the button-mushroom kit’s instructions for each stage and keep conditions steady, with ventilation and no direct sun.
The compost can generate its own heat while the mycelium spreads. Avoid overheating and follow the supplier’s temperature range; a single upper temperature limit is not reliable for every strain or kit.
Cropping around 16–18°C suits many button-mushroom kits, but follow the supplier’s range. Keep the casing lightly moist with careful watering, never saturated.
Harvesting & storage
Pick button mushrooms at the size you prefer, before the veil opens for closed buttons or later for open caps. Crops arrive in flushes with rests between them; the start and duration depend on the kit and growing conditions.
For cultivated button mushrooms, twist gently to lift the mushroom with minimal disturbance. Trim off dirty stem bases and remove broken remnants; refill holes with suitable casing where the kit recommends it.
After the final crop, compost healthy spent substrate or use it as a soil improver. Mushroom compost can contain substantial soluble salts, so weather it before use near seedlings or salt-sensitive plants. Start new crops with fresh prepared material.
Between flushes, maintain the kit’s recommended moisture with clean water and wait for the next crop. Once exhausted, remove old substrate, wash and rinse reusable containers, and let them dry before starting again.

Troubles

Protect young seedlings and keep roots growing steadily. Check leaf damage, bolting and root quality separately. Confirm nutrient problems before adding trace elements, and lift sound roots before prolonged autumn wet or severe frost.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

BEETROOT

Blackleg
RECOGNISE

Seedlings blacken, shrivel and may collapse. Crowding, poor drainage and excess moisture favour seedling disease.

ACT

Remove collapsed seedlings. Correct excess wetness; affected plants will not recover.

PREVENT

Sow thinly in well-drained ground. For modules, use fresh seed compost and clean trays; avoid overwatering.

BEETROOT

Bolting
RECOGNISE

A flower stem forms before a useful root develops. Cold during early growth or hot, dry conditions can trigger bolting.

ACT

Remove bolted plants; sow replacements when conditions are suitable.

PREVENT

Use Boltardy for protected early sowings, or sow as spring warms. Maintain moisture and thin direct sowings promptly.

BEETROOT

Leaf Spot

Spotted leaves

RECOGNISE

Brown spots may develop pale centres that fall out. Light spotting may have little effect; severe leaf loss can check growth.

ACT

Remove badly affected leaves; minor spotting seldom needs intervention.

PREVENT

Rotate crops and prepare adequately nourished soil before sowing.

BEETROOT

Fanging
RECOGNISE

Roots divide or fork, often where fresh manure, stones or poorly prepared heavy soil interrupt growth.

ACT

Existing forked roots will not straighten.

PREVENT

Use ground manured for a previous crop, or well-rotted compost added in autumn. Remove stones and prepare the soil well.

BEETROOT

Beet Leaf Miner (Mangold Fly)

Blistered leaves

RECOGNISE

White grubs mine leaves, making pale blotches that turn brown. Early summer damage checks young plants; flies are active April–September.

ACT

Remove mined leaves, or crush grubs within mines. Check leaf undersides for clusters of white eggs.

PREVENT

Use insect-proof mesh on a rotated site: overwintering flies can emerge beneath covers on old ground.

Blackened roots

Check soil pH and confirm the shortage. Seek an organic-compatible correction if needed; damaged roots will not recover.

Dark, decaying areas can develop on roots left in wet autumn soil. Appearance alone does not identify the cause.

ACT

Lift promptly. Discard rotting roots and check stored roots regularly.

Lift before prolonged wet or severe frost. Avoid harvest damage and store only sound roots in a cool, frost-free place.

Rolled leaves

RECOGNISE

Yellow areas between veins may become brown; leaf edges roll inward. Manganese deficiency is one possible cause.

ACT

Check pH and moisture and confirm the cause. Seek an organic-compatible correction if needed; other deficiencies can look similar.

PREVENT

Avoid over-liming; maintain good soil condition and steady growth.

Harvest mature split heads promptly; do not expect the split to heal.

PREVENT

Keep moisture steady and avoid leaving mature heads standing too long, especially before severe cold.

BRUSSELS SPROUTS

Blown Brussels Sprouts
RECOGNISE

Sprouts become open and leafy rather than tight buttons. Loose soil, drought, crowding and other growth checks contribute.

ACT

Pick small tender blown sprouts for prompt use; remove larger spoiled ones.

PREVENT

Firm plants well, give adequate space and water in dry weather. An F1 variety may produce firmer sprouts.

CAULIFLOWER

Button Cauliflowers
RECOGNISE

Very small heads form early and soon run to seed after checks to growth. Pests, poor soil, crowding, drought or nutrient shortages may contribute.

ACT

Established button heads will not become normal full-sized curds.

PREVENT

Use rich firm soil, proper spacing and hardened-off plants. Water consistently and prevent early pest damage. Investigate suspected deficiencies before treatment.

CAULIFLOWER

Whiptail

Narrow leaves

RECOGNISE

Thin, strap-like cauliflower leaves and very small or absent heads suggest molybdenum deficiency, often associated with acid soil.

ACT

Confirm the cause and test soil pH; seek advice on an organic-compatible correction if needed.

PREVENT

Test pH and correct excessive acidity before the next cauliflower crop.

Brown curds

RECOGNISE

Cauliflower leaves distort; curds may be small, brown-spotted or bitter. These signs alone do not confirm boron shortage.

ACT

Confirm the deficiency and check pH and moisture. Seek an organic-compatible correction; damaged curds will not repair themselves.

PREVENT

Improve soil with compost and keep growth steady. Excess boron is toxic: never dose by guesswork.

Mottling between veins

RECOGNISE

Older leaves develop yellowing between veins, sometimes followed by reddish or brown areas.

ACT

Confirm the problem and check watering, pH and feeding. Seek advice on a suitable organic-compatible magnesium amendment if needed.

PREVENT

Improve light soil with compost. Avoid excessive potassium feeding, which can reduce magnesium uptake.

Frost

Cold-damaged leaves

RECOGNISE

Severe cold damages exposed heads and leaves, especially where plants are loose. Winter cabbages and savoys tolerate some frost.

ACT

Allow healthy growing points to recover. Remove rotting leaves and gently re-firm lifted roots.

PREVENT

Plant securely and earth up where needed. Harvest sound mature heads before severe weather when appropriate.

Cabbage Stem Flea Beetle

Tunnelled stems

RECOGNISE

Wilting plants may have cream-coloured grubs inside stems. Attacks occur mainly from August to October.

ACT

Remove badly infested plants after checking inside stems to confirm the cause.

PREVENT

Rotate away from affected ground rather than repeating brassicas there next season.

Manganese Deficiency
RECOGNISE

Yellowing between veins with curled or scorched edges can resemble other nutrient problems; one leaf is not enough for a firm diagnosis.

ACT

Check soil conditions and confirm the cause. Seek advice on an organic-compatible correction if required.

PREVENT

Maintain good soil condition and avoid unnecessary liming.

Carrot and Parsnip
Troubles

Carrots and parsnips share several root pests and diseases. Carrots are especially vulnerable to carrot fly; parsnips also suffer from old seed and canker. Start with fresh seed, deep well-prepared soil and a clean seedbed. Avoid fresh manure; use resistant varieties where available.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

PARSNIP

Old Seed / Poor Germination
RECOGNISE

Old seed, cold or dry soil and deep sowing can all delay or prevent emergence. Check conditions before resowing.

ACT

Sow again with fresh seed if the season still allows.

PREVENT

Use fresh seed each year. Keep the drill moist until seedlings emerge; a few radish seeds can mark the row.

CARROT

Green Top
RECOGNISE

Sunlight turns exposed carrot crowns green. Unlike green potatoes, green carrots are not harmful, but look unsightly.

PREVENT

Earth up around exposed crowns during the growing season.

PARSNIP

Parsnip Rust Fungus
RECOGNISE

Rust-coloured crown damage may resemble staining or canker; the precise cause needs confirmation.

ACT

Lift and discard badly affected roots.

PREVENT

Improve drainage, avoid root injury and seek a diagnosis before choosing a long crop break.

CARROT

Clayburn
RECOGNISE

Carrot surface damage associated with clay; check for pests or rot. The cause is uncertain.

ACT

Inspect affected roots; seek identification for recurring damage. Discard active decay.

PREVENT

Prepare well-drained, workable soil; use a raised bed where necessary.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Carrot Fly

Tunnelled roots

RECOGNISE

Leaves turn reddish, then yellow. Maggots tunnel in carrots or damage parsnip surfaces. Seedlings may die; roots may rot.

ACT

No cure. Minor surface damage on large parsnips may be trimmed away.

PREVENT

Cover completely with insect-proof mesh on rotated ground. Sow thinly. Carrots sown after mid-May or lifted before late August may avoid peak attacks.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Fanging

Forked roots

RECOGNISE

Roots fork when tips meet stones, compaction or injury. Fresh manure and uneven seedbeds can contribute.

ACT

There is no treatment for an already forked root.

PREVENT

Prepare workable soil, remove larger stones and avoid compaction or fresh manure before sowing.

CARROT

Small Roots
RECOGNISE

Crowding, drought, poor soil or pest damage can keep roots small. First check variety and maturity.

ACT

Check spacing, water and root health. Thin carefully and correct confirmed poor fertility.

PREVENT

Prepare workable soil in advance; maintain suitable spacing and steady moisture.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Splitting

Split roots

RECOGNISE

Roots split after heavy rain or watering follows a dry spell. Leaving mature roots in wet autumn soil also increases the risk.

ACT

There is no cure. Use split roots immediately; they will not store.

PREVENT

Water regularly and deeply in drought. Mulch with compost to steady moisture. Where splitting recurs, lift maincrop carrots before prolonged wet weather.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Sclerotinia Rot

Mouldy roots

RECOGNISE

Soft root or crown rot develops white cottony mould, sometimes with black resting bodies. Both growing crops and stored roots can be affected.

ACT

Remove infected plants and rotten stored roots promptly; keep them out of home compost.

PREVENT

Store sound roots and check regularly. Clear infected debris, improve drainage and avoid moving contaminated soil.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Carrot-Willow Aphid

Distorted leaves

RECOGNISE

Greenfly cause distorted, discoloured, stunted leaves, especially in warm, dry summers. They can also transmit motley dwarf virus.

ACT

Tolerate small colonies; squash damaging colonies and encourage natural predators.

PREVENT

Inspect young crops and maintain steady growth. Aphid management cannot guarantee protection from viruses.

CARROT

Black Rot

Blackened carrot roots

RECOGNISE

Large black patches develop on stored carrots, often with no obvious symptoms before harvest.

ACT

Remove and destroy diseased roots promptly.

PREVENT

Store only sound roots in a cool, ventilated place and inspect regularly. Do not grow carrots on the same land next year. Avoid reusing a problem storage site year after year.

CARROT

Carrot Motley Dwarf

Discoloured leaves

RECOGNISE

Yellow mottling, red outer leaves and stunting may indicate carrot motley dwarf, an aphid-transmitted virus complex.

ACT

Confirm the cause and remove badly affected plants; infected plants cannot be cured.

PREVENT

Inspect young growth, encourage aphid predators and remove damaging colonies. Virus spread can still occur.

Blackened parsnip roots

RECOGNISE

Brown or black rot and cracking around the crown. Damage can spread downwards in wet, heavy soil; large roots suffer most.

ACT

No cure. Trim damage and use sound roots promptly. Destroy badly rotten roots; do not store them.

PREVENT

Mouldy roots

RECOGNISE

Foliage may yellow slightly. Lifted roots show a felt-like coating of purple fungal threads, especially on the lower parts.

ACT

There is no cure. Destroy diseased roots.

PREVENT

Keep affected roots out of storage. Remove infected roots, avoid moving soil and seek crop-break advice if losses recur.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Swift Moth

Hollowed-out roots

RECOGNISE

Soil-living caterpillars hollow out roots and may move backwards when disturbed. Affected plants can lose vigour.

ACT

Inspect soil beside damaged roots; hand-remove caterpillars. Discard badly damaged or rotting roots.

PREVENT

Check vulnerable plants. For recurring losses, consider suitable biological nematodes with supplier guidance.

Celery
Troubles

Keep celery and celeriac growing steadily: moist roots, good drainage and healthy seedlings matter. Check leaves for miners and spots, and inspect stalks and hearts for damage. Celery needs moisture, but wet, crowded conditions can also favour disease.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

CELERY / CELERIAC

Bolting
RECOGNISE

Cold exposure or checks during young growth can trigger premature flowering in celery or celeriac.

ACT

There is no way to reverse bolting.

PREVENT

Keep roots moist, harden plants gradually and wait until frost risk has passed before planting.

CELERY

Splitting

Split stalks

RECOGNISE

Vertical splits spoil stalks after dry soil, uneven growth or excessive nitrogen.

ACT

Existing splits cannot heal.

PREVENT

Water steadily, improve soil with mature compost and avoid excessive nitrogen feeding.

CELERY / CELERIAC

Damping Off
RECOGNISE

Seedlings develop a watery, soft stem base and topple over, often in wet, poorly aired trays.

ACT

Remove affected seedlings; improve ventilation and avoid splashing the remainder.

PREVENT

Sow thinly in clean compost. Keep it just damp, air trays and remove condensation from covers.

CELERY / CELERIAC

Celery Leaf Spot (Blight)

Spotted leaves

RECOGNISE

Brown or yellow-brown spots start on outer leaflets and spread in wet conditions. Infection can arrive on seed or seedlings.

ACT

Remove affected leaves and discard badly diseased plants.

PREVENT

Buy healthy seed and plants. Reject spotted seedlings; allow airflow and avoid splashing foliage.

CELERY / CELERIAC

Celery Fly (Leaf Miner)

Blistered leaves

RECOGNISE

Broad pale leaf mines dry into brown papery blotches. Young celery may become stunted and bitter; celeriac is also affected.

ACT

Tolerate light damage; pinch out badly mined leaf parts on uncovered plants.

PREVENT

Check young plants from May. Use insect-proof mesh on a rotated bed, so flies cannot emerge beneath it.

CELERY

Rotten hearts

RECOGNISE

The inner heart becomes a slimy brown mass. Wounds from slugs, frost or cultivation allow bacterial rot to enter.

ACT

Discard diseased plants; rotten hearts cannot recover.

RECOGNISE

Irregular holes spoil celery stalks; celeriac roots may also be holed. Woodlice sometimes occupy existing damage.

Hand-remove slugs after dark. At harvest, trim damage and use sound tissue promptly; discard rot.

Keep damp debris away from vulnerable plants, check regularly and harvest before damage becomes severe.

Cucurbit
Troubles

Cucumbers, courgettes, marrows and squash need warmth and steady moisture, but dislike cold, waterlogged roots. Check pollination before blaming disease for poor fruit set. Under glass, balance humidity with ventilation; handle storage squash carefully.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

No Fruit
RECOGNISE

Poor pollination, cold or root stress can limit fruit set. Check cucumber variety needs.

ACT

On a dry morning, transfer pollen from a male flower to female flowers. Keep roots moist.

PREVENT

Do not apply this to greenhouse cucumbers grown for unpollinated fruit; follow the variety instructions.

CUCUMBER, GREENHOUSE

Poor Yield
RECOGNISE

Greenhouse cucumbers may lose vigour after the first harvest, especially if fruit becomes over-mature or roots are stressed.

ACT

Pick frequently, water steadily and feed at the recommended rate. Keep mulch clear of the stem base and check drainage.

PREVENT

Maintain warmth, steady moisture and healthy roots; do not leave mature fruit on the plant.

CUCUMBER, GREENHOUSE / CUCUMBER, OUTDOOR / COURGETTES AND MARROWS / SQUASHES AND PUMPKINS

Withering of Young Fruit
RECOGNISE

Young fruit stops swelling and shrivels. Check pollination needs, root health and temperatures.

ACT

Remove failed fruit. Check soil moisture and drainage before watering; do not impose a fixed dry week.

PREVENT

Keep growth steady and protect roots from cold, drought and waterlogging.

CUCUMBER, GREENHOUSE / CUCUMBER, OUTDOOR / COURGETTES AND MARROWS / SQUASHES AND PUMPKINS

Sun Scald

Papery patches

RECOGNISE

Pale brown, papery patches develop at leaf margins after excessive sun; dry tissue shrinks.

ACT

Scorched tissue will not recover.

PREVENT

Provide greenhouse shading and ventilation while keeping roots evenly moist.

CUCUMBER, GREENHOUSE / CUCUMBER, OUTDOOR / COURGETTES AND MARROWS / SQUASHES AND PUMPKINS

Bitterness
RECOGNISE

Stress can make cucumbers bitter. Unwanted pollination affects some greenhouse varieties; outdoor types have different requirements.

ACT

Do not eat unusually bitter cucumbers, courgettes or squash. Discard them; cutting, rubbing or cooking is not a reliable remedy.

PREVENT

Follow cucumber variety instructions: keep seedless greenhouse crops unpollinated; retain male flowers where outdoor types need pollen. Keep growth steady.

Florence Fennel
Troubles

Florence fennel needs steady growth to form juicy bulbs. Check sowing time and root moisture first. Harvest mature bulbs promptly: prolonged damp and frost can spoil their outer sheaths.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

FLORENCE FENNEL

Bolting / Stemmy Bulbs
RECOGNISE

A narrow bulb elongates into a flowering stem instead of swelling. Once stemmy, it is unlikely to become fleshy.

ACT

Harvest usable parts promptly, trimming tough stems.

PREVENT

For outdoor UK sowing, June or July is usually safer. Choose a bolt-resistant variety and avoid drought or crowding.

RECOGNISE

Dry soil checks growth, leaving small, less juicy bulbs and increasing the risk of bolting.

Water thoroughly and mulch. Harvest small usable bulbs if growth has stalled.

Use moisture-retentive soil, thin promptly and water steadily as bulbs swell. A 5 cm / 2 in compost mulch can help.

Lower Sheath Rot
RECOGNISE

Outer bulb sheaths can soften and rot in wet conditions or after delayed harvest. Check inside before use.

ACT

Lift promptly. Discard rotten tissue; use only firm, sound parts and discard extensively rotted bulbs.

PREVENT

Avoid waterlogging and harvest mature bulbs before prolonged damp causes deterioration.

FLORENCE FENNEL

Frost Damage
RECOGNISE

Exposed bulbs lose quality after frost and may become water-soaked or soft. They do not store well.

ACT

Lift promptly and use only sound flesh; discard soft or rotten bulbs.

PREVENT

Harvest before hard frost. Keep sound harvested bulbs cool and frost-free for short-term use.

RECOGNISE

ACT

Check after dark or in damp weather and hand-remove slugs and snails.

Damaged roots

PREVENT

Rotten stems

Large grey, green or brown caterpillars sever young plants at soil level at night. Older roots may be gnawed; June-July is a risk period.

ACT

Search soil beside damaged plants and hand-remove caterpillars.

PREVENT

Check vulnerable young crops; use biological controls only when suitable for the pest and soil conditions.

LETTUCE

Lettuce Root Maggot

Tunnelled roots

RECOGNISE

Root-tunnelling larvae may cause lettuce wilt and stunting. Inspect roots and confirm the insect.

ACT

Remove affected plants. Seek identification: other root problems cause similar wilting.

PREVENT

Inspect unexplained wilt, clear affected debris and use healthy plants and clean growing media.
