Lettuce
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

LETTUCE / ENDIVE

Mosaic Virus

Mottled leaves

RECOGNISE

Yellow or pale-green mottling, nearly transparent veins and stunting suggest mosaic virus, which aphids can spread.

ACT

Remove infected plants; virus has no cure.

PREVENT

Use healthy seed and plants. Watch aphids and encourage predators; this does not guarantee protection.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 3

Onion & Leek
Troubles

Check alliums at the leaf base as well as above ground. Feeding damage, rot and growth checks can look alike. Use sound bulbs with thick necks or splits promptly; store only dry, healthy bulbs. White rot needs particular care to avoid spreading soil.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Bolting
RECOGNISE

A premature flower stalk forms, often after cold or checked growth. Oversized sets can be more susceptible.

ACT

Pinch out small flower stems without loosening bulbs; use affected bulbs early.

PREVENT

Choose suitable small or heat-treated sets, plant at the recommended season and avoid growth checks.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Saddleback

Bulbs split at base.

RECOGNISE

Bulbs split at the base, often after heavy rain or watering follows prolonged drought.

ACT

Use sound split bulbs promptly; they will not store well.

PREVENT

Keep growth steady with watering during dry summer spells.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Set Division
RECOGNISE

Onion sets may form twin bulbs; large sets and growth checks can contribute. Shallots naturally form clusters.

PREVENT

Use suitable onion sets, plant in season and maintain steady growth. Shallot division is normal.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Birds Pulling Sets

Newly planted onion sets are pulled out of the soil just as they begin to grow.

RECOGNISE

Newly planted onion sets are pulled out before they establish. Birds may investigate their exposed dry tips.

ACT

Replant sound lifted sets promptly before their roots dry out.

PREVENT

Firm sets at normal depth and guard with secure netting until rooted. Check for trapped wildlife.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Onion Fly

Tunnelled bulbs with 1/4 in. white maggots.

RECOGNISE

Yellow, drooping leaves accompany maggots feeding at bulb bases. Seedlings may die; older plants fail to develop.

ACT

Remove badly affected plants and infested bulbs.

PREVENT

Use insect-proof mesh with rotation. Clear crop debris; sets are less vulnerable than seedlings.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Drooping Leaves
RECOGNISE

Dark-green leaves may flop after excessive nitrogen. But drooping alone also needs checks for watering problems, pests or normal maturity.

ACT

Check roots and bulb bases before assuming a feeding problem.

PREVENT

Avoid fresh manure and excessive nitrogen; do not add fertiliser blindly.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 1

Onion & Leek
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS / LEEK / GARLIC

Stem & Bulb Eelworm

Twisted, swollen leaves.

RECOGNISE

Swollen, distorted leaves accompany soft bulbs. Microscopic stem and bulb nematodes may kill young plants.

ACT

Remove affected plants and seek a confirmed diagnosis.

PREVENT

Avoid moving infested soil. Plan a suitable rotation for the identified nematode and its host range.

LEEK

Smut
RECOGNISE

Black spots and blotches develop on leaves or bulbs of young plants; leaves thicken and twist. Leeks are particularly vulnerable.

ACT

Remove affected plants and seek confirmation.

PREVENT

Avoid moving affected soil and seek advice on a long crop break; the fungus can persist for years.

LEEK / GARLIC

Rust
RECOGNISE

Orange pustules mark leek and garlic leaves. Often cosmetic, heavy attacks yellow foliage and check growth.

ACT

Remove badly affected leaves and keep plants growing steadily.

PREVENT

Avoid crowding and excess nitrogen; water roots in dry spells and clear infected debris.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Bull Neck (Thick Neck)
RECOGNISE

Onions retain unusually thick, fleshy necks and store poorly. Excess nitrogen or deep sowing may contribute.

ACT

Use sound affected bulbs early; do not store them with well-ripened bulbs.

PREVENT

Avoid overfeeding and deep sowing. Additional feed will not cure a thick neck.

LEEK

White Tip
RECOGNISE

Leek tips turn white and papery in autumn; damage spreads down leaves and may stunt growth.

ACT

Remove badly diseased plants and affected debris.

PREVENT

Avoid an affected bed the following season; improve drainage and avoid prolonged leaf wetness.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Downy Mildew
RECOGNISE

Grey mould develops on onion leaves after wet weather, sometimes followed by black sootiness. Growth and storage quality suffer.

ACT

Remove badly affected material. Dry harvested bulbs thoroughly and keep suspect bulbs out of long storage.

PREVENT

Rotate, space well and improve drainage. Avoid nearby overwintered infected onions; choose resistant varieties.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 2

Onion & Leek
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

LEEK / ONIONS AND SHALLOTS / GARLIC

Leek Moth
RECOGNISE

Caterpillars feed inside leaves, leaving translucent patches or shredded tissue. Unlike fly maggots, they have heads and small legs.

ACT

Remove infested leaves. Badly damaged leeks may regrow if cut about 5 cm / 2 in above soil; remove the debris.

PREVENT

Protect young plants with fine mesh from planting out, using a rotated bed.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS / LEEK / GARLIC

White Rot (Mouldy Nose)
RECOGNISE

Yellowing leaves accompany root and bulb-base decay, white fungal fluff and tiny black resting bodies.

ACT

No cure: remove diseased plants and keep contaminated soil off clean ground.

PREVENT

Do not rely on normal rotation: resting bodies can survive at least 15 years. Grow alliums in clean ground.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Shanking
RECOGNISE

Yellowing, collapsing leaves and foul-smelling slime inside onion scales suggest soft rot.

ACT

Remove rotten bulbs promptly; keep them out of storage.

PREVENT

Avoid wounds and waterlogging. Dry sound bulbs well, store with airflow and inspect regularly.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Neck Rot
RECOGNISE

Grey mould starts around stored onion necks; bulbs become soft and rotten. Damp or damaged necks increase risk.

ACT

Check stores regularly and discard rotting bulbs immediately.

PREVENT

Dry thoroughly and store only sound, dry, thin-necked bulbs in a cool, airy place.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS / LEEK / GARLIC

Allium Leaf Miner

White specks or mines in leaves, followed by rotting; small orange-brown pupae may be found inside affected leaves or bulbs.

RECOGNISE

Rows of white leaf punctures precede internal mines and rot. Cream legless maggots or brown pupae occur inside stems and bulbs.

ACT

Remove badly infested plants and debris; internal larvae are hard to reach.

PREVENT

Use fine mesh and rotation, especially during adult activity in March-April and September-November.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 3

Oriental Leaves
Troubles

Pak choi, Chinese cabbage and related leaves grow best without checks. Keep roots moist, choose sowing times for the crop and variety, and protect young leaves from feeding damage. Harvest promptly if plants start flowering or weather threatens quality.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

ORIENTAL LEAVES

Flea Beetle
RECOGNISE

Tiny jumping beetles pepper young brassica leaves with round holes, especially in spring and early summer.

ACT

Water checked plants; accept small cosmetic holes where growth stays strong.

PREVENT

Protect early sowings with fine mesh or fleece. Late-summer sowings often escape the worst damage.

ORIENTAL LEAVES

Slugs
RECOGNISE

Ragged holes spoil succulent pak choi leaves and stems. Young plants and large outer leaves near damp soil are vulnerable.

ACT

Hand-remove slugs and clear badly damaged leaves.

PREVENT

Keep damp debris away, inspect young plants and harvest leaves regularly.

ORIENTAL LEAVES

Cabbage Caterpillars
RECOGNISE

Large holes and hidden caterpillars occur on brassica leaves and inside forming Chinese cabbage hearts.

ACT

Pick off eggs and caterpillars; remove badly damaged leaves.

PREVENT

Cover susceptible crops with fine mesh before butterflies lay eggs, keeping the edges secure.

ORIENTAL LEAVES

Root Disturbance in Pak Choi
RECOGNISE

Rough leaf-picking can loosen or uproot pak choi and damage its fragile roots.

ACT

Re-firm and water disturbed plants. Use uprooted plants promptly if they fail to re-establish.

PREVENT

Support the plant while picking small leaves, or cut the whole plant when picking is too disruptive.

ORIENTAL LEAVES

Bolting / Premature Flowering
RECOGNISE

A flower stem develops early, especially after heat, cold, drought or crowding. Leaves and stems become tougher.

ACT

Harvest tender leaves and shoots promptly before quality declines.

PREVENT

Pak choi favours spring or late summer; protect from cold and keep moist. Follow crop and variety sowing advice.

ORIENTAL LEAVES

Dryness and Poor Hearting
RECOGNISE

Chinese cabbage stays loose and coarse instead of forming a dense heart after drought, crowding or poor soil conditions.

ACT

Water thoroughly, mulch and thin; use loose leaves if plants remain checked.

PREVENT

Add compost and keep moist. Most varieties heart unaided; loosely tie only varieties that need it near maturity.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 1

Oriental Leaves
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

ORIENTAL LEAVES

Cabbage Root Fly on Leaf Radish
RECOGNISE

Cream maggots tunnel in brassica roots. Leaf radish foliage may still be usable even when its roots are spoiled.

ACT

Trim minor damage and discard badly affected roots.

PREVENT

Cover promptly with insect-proof mesh on a rotated bed; follow the crop sowing window.

ORIENTAL LEAVES

Frost and Winter Decline
RECOGNISE

Chinese cabbage and leaf radish lose quality in winter cold. Some mustards tolerate light frost better.

ACT

Harvest sound leaves or heads before hard frost; discard soft, rotting tissue.

PREVENT

Use fleece or protected cropping and choose hardier leaves for late crops. Time harvest for local weather.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 2

Potato
Troubles

Start with healthy seed potatoes and keep growth steady. Check foliage for blight and frost, then inspect tubers at harvest and in store. Earth up well, lift carefully and store only sound, dry potatoes in a dark, cool, airy, frost-free place.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

POTATO

Spindly Sprouts
RECOGNISE

Long, weak shoots develop when seed tubers are too warm or dark. Threadlike shoots even in good conditions may indicate disease or frost damage.

PREVENT

Buy healthy seed potatoes and sprout them in a bright, cool, frost-free place.

POTATO

Soft Tubers
RECOGNISE

Tubers may feel soft and rubbery after severe drought, despite an apparently sound skin. Softness can also have other causes.

ACT

Check for decay; discard rotten tubers.

PREVENT

Water thoroughly during drought to avoid severe growth checks.

POTATO

Gapping
RECOGNISE

A gap in the row may mean a seed tuber failed to sprout after decay, damage or poor storage.

ACT

Check failed planting positions for the cause.

PREVENT

Plant sound seed tubers and protect them from frost, damage and decay before planting.

POTATO

Splitting

Tuber troubles

RECOGNISE

Deep growth cracks make tubers awkward to peel and more likely to rot in store.

ACT

Use sound cracked tubers promptly; discard decay.

PREVENT

Keep plants watered during dry spells to avoid abrupt changes in growth.

POTATO

Potato Blight

Brown-blotched leaves

RECOGNISE

Rapidly spreading brown, collapsing leaves and stem lesions develop in warm, wet weather. Tubers may later rot.

ACT

At stem lesions or about a quarter of leaves affected, cut off foliage. Wait about two weeks, then lift; avoid storage.

PREVENT

Earth up, remove volunteers and use healthy seed and resistant varieties.

POTATO

Frost

Blackened, collapsed leaves

RECOGNISE

Late spring frost blackens and collapses leaves, especially on early crops. Unfrozen lower stems often regrow.

ACT

Allow time for new shoots. Remove collapsed growth only if it is rotting.

PREVENT

Cover emerging shoots before forecast frost with soil, fleece or cloches.

IMPERIAL · 1

Potato
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

POTATO

Leaf Roll Virus

Rolled leaflets

RECOGNISE

Leaflets roll upwards and become hard and brittle. Plants are stunted and yield poorly.

ACT

There is no cure for infected plants.

PREVENT

Use certified seed potatoes. Watch aphids and encourage predators; aphid control cannot guarantee protection.

POTATO

Mosaic Virus

Mottled leaves

RECOGNISE

Yellow or pale-green mottling covers leaves, sometimes with brown streaks. Symptoms vary with virus and potato variety.

ACT

There is no cure for infected plants.

PREVENT

Use certified seed potatoes and avoid saving seed from affected crops. Encourage aphid predators.

POTATO

Aphid (Greenfly)

Insects on leaves

RECOGNISE

Aphid colonies weaken foliage in warm, dry weather. Their most serious effect is spreading viruses.

ACT

Tolerate small colonies; squash or rinse off damaging clusters where practical.

PREVENT

Encourage natural predators and inspect plants. Aphid control does not guarantee virus prevention.

POTATO

Capsid Bug
RECOGNISE

Small brown feeding spots become holes; young shoots and leaflets may be distorted or crinkled.

ACT

Usually little effect on yield: tolerate minor damage.

PREVENT

Check new growth and encourage natural enemies.

POTATO

Magnesium Deficiency

Browning between veins

RECOGNISE

Yellowing between greener veins later becomes brown and brittle. Growth may be checked; other problems can look similar.

ACT

Check soil, roots and feeding before treating a suspected deficiency.

PREVENT

Use balanced nutrition guided by need; avoid excessive potash, which can restrict magnesium uptake.

POTATO

Blackleg

Blackened stems

RECOGNISE

Stem bases turn black at or below soil level. Leaves yellow and wilt, then the plant withers, especially in wet, heavy soil.

ACT

Remove affected plants; there is no cure.

PREVENT

Plant sound seed tubers, never soft or rotten ones. Cutting seed tubers increases infection risk.

Potato
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

POTATO

Rosy Rustic Moth

Tunnelled stems

RECOGNISE

Caterpillars hollow out stems and plants die back early, particularly on newly cultivated ground.

ACT

Remove badly infested plants and larvae.

PREVENT

Inspect affected stems; no reliable general preventive measure.

POTATO

Potato Cyst Eelworm

Withered lower leaves

RECOGNISE

Weak, stunted plants wilt by day and yield poorly. Tiny cysts may be visible on roots where potatoes are repeatedly grown.

ACT

Seek confirmation; there is no cure for the affected crop.

PREVENT

Use long rotations and suitable resistant varieties. Remove volunteers and avoid moving infested soil.

POTATO

Slugs

Tuber troubles

RECOGNISE

Irregular holes and cavities spoil tubers, particularly maincrops left in damp, heavy soil late in the season.

ACT

Lift before damage worsens. Use only sound tissue promptly and discard rot.

PREVENT

Choose less susceptible varieties and avoid slug-sheltering mulch. Harvest once mature.

POTATO

Wireworm

Tuber troubles

RECOGNISE

Narrow tunnels run through tubers; hard, yellow-brown larvae may be found, especially on former grassland.

ACT

There is no repair for damaged tubers.

PREVENT

Avoid heavily infested ground for potatoes. Lift mature crops promptly and remove larvae found during cultivation.

POTATO

Common Scab

Tuber troubles

RECOGNISE

Rough corky patches mark tuber skins. Usually cosmetic, it is favoured by dry, alkaline soil.

ACT

Existing scabs cannot be cured.

PREVENT

Do not lime just before potatoes. Keep soil moist during tuber formation and choose resistant varieties.

POTATO

Powdery Scab

Tuber troubles

RECOGNISE

Scabby pustules break into powdery lesions, especially in wet, heavy soil. Less common than common scab.

ACT

Affected tubers cannot be cured.

PREVENT

Rotate crops and choose less susceptible varieties; avoid poorly drained ground.

Potato
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

POTATO

Spraing

Tuber troubles

RECOGNISE

Brown arcs, rings or streaks occur inside otherwise normal-looking tubers. Virus infection is a common cause; similar browning needs diagnosis.

ACT

No cure for affected tubers.

PREVENT

Use healthy seed and less susceptible varieties. Seek advice if recurring; rotation alone may not clear the cause.

POTATO

Blight (Tubers)

Tuber troubles

RECOGNISE

Blight causes reddish-brown decay beneath tuber skins, often followed by soft rot. Light infections may only appear in store.

ACT

Do not store affected tubers; discard decay and use sound tubers from the crop promptly.

PREVENT

Earth up. After removing blighted foliage, wait about two weeks before lifting.

POTATO

Dry Rot

Tuber troubles

RECOGNISE

Stored tubers develop dry, sunken decay, often following bruises or wounds at lifting.

ACT

Remove and discard affected tubers.

PREVENT

Lift gently, dry before storage and store only sound tubers in cool, dark, airy, frost-free conditions.

POTATO

Soft Rot

Tuber troubles

RECOGNISE

Damaged, wet, frosted or diseased stored tubers become slimy and foul-smelling.

ACT

Discard rotting tubers immediately and check neighbouring potatoes.

PREVENT

Store only sound, dry, undamaged tubers; keep cool, dark, airy and frost-free.

POTATO

Gangrene

Tuber troubles

RECOGNISE

Stored tubers develop sunken decay; internal tissue becomes dry, hollow and rotted.

ACT

Remove affected tubers from store.

PREVENT

Store only sound, healthy tubers and keep the store airy and frost-free.

POTATO

Hollow Heart

Tuber troubles

RECOGNISE

Large tubers have an internal hollow, often following uneven growth and wet conditions after drought.

ACT

Existing cavities cannot heal; discard any tuber with rot.

PREVENT

Keep watering steady during dry spells.

Potato
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

POTATO

Poor Quality
RECOGNISE

Flavour and texture vary with variety, maturity and storage. Internal blackheart is different from darkening after cooking.

ACT

Check variety, harvest timing and storage before assuming a nutrient problem.

PREVENT

Choose varieties for the cooking method and store correctly; do not add potash as a universal remedy.

POTATO

Wart Disease

Tuber troubles

RECOGNISE

Cauliflower-like growths develop around tuber eyes and darken with age. Other disorders can resemble this controlled disease.

ACT

Report suspicion promptly to the plant-health authority; await instructions before moving or disposing of material.

PREVENT

Use certified seed and follow official restrictions; do not simply replant affected ground.

POTATO

Colorado Beetle

Striped beetles on leaves

RECOGNISE

Adults have yellow wing cases with black lengthwise stripes. Red-orange, black-spotted larvae also eat foliage.

ACT

Contain a suspected beetle securely; do not release it. Report promptly to the plant-health authority.

PREVENT

Inspect plants and follow official instructions. In England/Wales contact APHA: 0300 1000 313.

IMPERIAL · 5

Spinach
Troubles

True spinach bolts readily in hot, dry weather; damp, crowded leaves favour mildew. Check leaf undersides as well as new growth. Spinach beet and tender New Zealand spinach are different crops: the frost advice here applies specifically to New Zealand spinach.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

SPINACH

Bolting
RECOGNISE

Long days and warm weather encourage true spinach to bolt, especially after drought or other growth checks.

ACT

Compost bolted plants and use the next sowing.

PREVENT

Choose bolt-resistant varieties, thin early and keep soil moist with watering and mulch. Sow short rows in succession.

SPINACH / BEET, LEAF

Leaf Spot

Spotted leaves

RECOGNISE

Small spots have pale centres and dark brown or purple margins. Centres may fall out and spots merge; several diseases can look similar.

ACT

Pick off affected leaves and discard badly diseased plants.

PREVENT

Rotate crops, clear diseased debris and maintain balanced organic fertility without overfeeding.

SPINACH

New Zealand Spinach Frost Damage
RECOGNISE

Frost damages the fleshy leaves and stems of tender New Zealand spinach, a summer substitute rather than true spinach.

ACT

Remove plants that fail to recover; resow or replant when conditions are warm.

PREVENT

Wait until frost danger has passed before sowing or planting outdoors. Protect from unexpected late frost.

SPINACH

Downy Mildew

Yellow patches

RECOGNISE

Yellow blotches above leaves correspond to grey-purple mould underneath. Damaged patches later turn brown.

ACT

Remove diseased leaves; discard badly affected plants and resow a short row.

PREVENT

Thin promptly, provide drainage and avoid prolonged leaf wetness. Rotate crops and sow small batches.

SPINACH

Spinach Blight

Rolled leaves

RECOGNISE

Young leaves become narrow, puckered, yellow-mottled and rolled inward. Cucumber mosaic virus can cause these signs.

ACT

Confirm the cause and remove infected plants; there is no cure for virus.

PREVENT

Remove weed hosts and encourage aphid predators. Control does not guarantee prevention of virus transmission.

Spinach
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

SPINACH / BEET, LEAF

Manganese Deficiency

Yellowed leaves

RECOGNISE

Yellow areas between greener veins, sometimes with curled margins, can indicate nutrient shortage. Similar symptoms have other causes.

ACT

Check soil pH, roots and watering before adding nutrients. Seek advice on an organic-compatible correction if confirmed.

PREVENT

Avoid unnecessary lime and improve soil condition. Alkaline soil can make manganese unavailable.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 2

Tomato
Troubles

Check leaves, stems and fruit separately. Steady watering and sensible feeding prevent many fruit disorders. Ventilate greenhouse crops; watch outdoor plants closely during damp weather. Confirm the cause before removing plants or adding nutrients.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Leaf Roll
RECOGNISE

Leaf rolling is often physiological. Check water and temperature; investigate mottling, stunting, pests or severe distortion.

ACT

No treatment is needed if pests and disease are absent.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Virus

Distorted or discoloured leaves

RECOGNISE

Mottled, curled or fern-like foliage, dark stem streaks and stunting can indicate virus. Fruit may be mottled or bronzed.

ACT

Remove affected plants and clean hands and tools before handling healthy plants.

PREVENT

Buy healthy plants, monitor aphids and wash hands and tools between plants. Avoid handling plants after tobacco use.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Tomato Leaf Mould

Brown mould patches

RECOGNISE

Yellow patches above leaves correspond to grey-brown mould underneath, usually starting low down on greenhouse plants.

ACT

Pick off infected leaves and dispose of crop debris after harvest.

PREVENT

Ventilate well and water roots without wetting foliage. Avoid dry compost; resistant varieties may help.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Root Rot
RECOGNISE

Brown, decayed or corky roots accompany wilting. Poor drainage favours some root diseases; confirm recurring losses.

ACT

Remove collapsed plants and correct drainage; rotten roots cannot be repaired.

PREVENT

Avoid waterlogging. Where losses recur, use fresh peat-free compost in clean containers.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Grey Mould (Botrytis)

Grey furry patches

RECOGNISE

Fuzzy grey mould starts on damaged stems or decaying tissue. Infected flower stalks may shed fruit.

ACT

Remove infected tissue promptly; discard badly affected plants.

PREVENT

Ventilate, avoid crowding and clear dying leaves and fruit. Keep pruning wounds and foliage dry.

Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Potato Blight

Dark brown blotches

RECOGNISE

Brown leaf patches spread rapidly in damp weather; stems may blacken and foliage collapse. Fruit can become infected.

ACT

Remove affected plants when disease is established. Check harvested fruit for developing rot.

PREVENT

Keep foliage dry, space plants for airflow and consider resistant varieties or rain protection with ventilation.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Foot Rot

Brown stem bases

RECOGNISE

Brown decay at the stem base can collapse seedlings or older plants.

ACT

Remove badly affected plants. Check drainage and seek a diagnosis if losses recur.

PREVENT

Use clean pots and fresh seed compost. Avoid overwatering and known infected soil.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Stem Rot (Didymella)

Brown stem bases

RECOGNISE

A sunken brown stem canker with black dots develops on mature plants; lower leaves yellow.

ACT

Remove badly affected plants and infected debris.

PREVENT

Clean supports and equipment between crops. Avoid stem injuries and persistent wetness.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Verticillium Wilt

Brown-streaked tissue

RECOGNISE

Leaves wilt in warmth, sometimes recovering overnight. Lower leaves yellow; cut stems may show brown internal streaks.

ACT

There is no cure. Confirm the cause before removing badly affected plants.

PREVENT

Avoid infected soil; use fresh compost in clean containers where soil-borne disease recurs.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Eelworm

Swellings on roots

RECOGNISE

Stunting, discoloured leaves and wilting may accompany small cysts or larger swellings on roots.

ACT

Confirm the pest before discarding badly affected plants.

PREVENT

Avoid infested soil and contaminated root balls. Identify the nematode before planning a rotation; hosts and persistence differ.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE

Greenhouse Whitefly

Tiny white insects beneath leaves

RECOGNISE

Tiny white adults fly from leaf undersides. Sap feeding, sticky honeydew and sooty mould can weaken plants.

ACT

Introduce suitable biological control early, such as Encarsia, following supplier temperature and timing advice.

PREVENT

Check new plants and leaf undersides regularly. Use yellow cards for monitoring, away from released beneficial insects.

IMPERIAL · 2

Tomato
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Aphids

Sap-sucking insects on soft growth

RECOGNISE

Colonies on tender growth suck sap; vigorous plants may outgrow light spring infestations.

ACT

Squash small damaging colonies by hand; allow natural predators to help.

PREVENT

Maintain steady growth and balanced fertility. Avoid stress and excessive nitrogen.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Tomato Moth
RECOGNISE

Green or brown caterpillars chew leaves and tunnel into fruit or stems.

ACT

Hand-pick caterpillars and discard damaged fruit.

PREVENT

Inspect foliage and fruit regularly; remove young caterpillars before they enter fruit.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Cutworm

Young plants cut off at soil level

RECOGNISE

Young plants are bitten through just above soil level soon after planting.

ACT

Look just below the soil near cut stems and remove caterpillars. Replace plants that cannot recover.

PREVENT

Protect vulnerable transplants with collars and check them regularly.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Blossom End Rot
RECOGNISE

A dark, sunken blossom-end patch develops when too little calcium reaches the fruit, often after irregular watering.

ACT

Spoiled tissue will not recover. Remove affected fruit and stabilise watering.

PREVENT

Keep roots evenly moist, provide adequate root space and avoid overfeeding.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Split Fruit
RECOGNISE

Skin cracks when fruit expands rapidly after rain or heavy watering follows a dry spell.

ACT

Existing splits cannot heal; discard fruit showing decay.

PREVENT

Keep roots evenly moist rather than alternating drought and soaking.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Blossom Drop
RECOGNISE

Flowers wither and fall after failed pollination or stress from heat, cold, humidity or irregular watering.

ACT

Check watering and greenhouse temperature. Gently tap flowering trusses to help pollen release.

PREVENT

Ventilate in heat and maintain even root moisture. Avoid prolonged wet foliage.

IMPERIAL · 3

Tomato
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Dry Set
RECOGNISE

Tiny fruitlets stop developing after poor pollination or flowering stress. Check heat, water supply and other symptoms.

ACT

Improve conditions for later flowers; stalled fruitlets may not resume growth.

PREVENT

Shade and ventilate in hot weather; keep root moisture steady.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Blotchy Ripening
RECOGNISE

Parts of fruit remain yellow or orange instead of ripening evenly; heat and inadequate potassium can contribute.

ACT

Existing uneven ripening may persist. Check heat and feeding.

PREVENT

Use greenhouse shading and ventilation, with measured organic-compatible tomato feeding. Do not overfeed.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Greenback
RECOGNISE

The shoulder around the stalk stays hard, green and unripe. Excess sun and feeding imbalance contribute.

ACT

Affected shoulders will not ripen normally.

PREVENT

Reduce excessive heat and sun, feed appropriately and consider resistant varieties.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Sun Scald
RECOGNISE

Pale, papery, sunken patches develop on fruit facing strong sun; leaves may also scorch.

ACT

Damaged tissue will not recover.

PREVENT

Shade and ventilate the greenhouse during strong sunshine; avoid exposing fruit by excessive leaf removal.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Hollow Fruit
RECOGNISE

Cut fruit has unusually large empty spaces. Poor pollination, temperature stress, feeding or weedkiller damage may contribute.

ACT

There is no repair for affected fruit.

PREVENT

Keep moisture and temperature steady, assist pollen release and feed appropriately. Prevent herbicide contamination.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Blight (Fruit)
RECOGNISE

Brown, shrunken fruit patches spread into rot, sometimes appearing after harvest. Damp-weather leaf blight often comes first.

ACT

Discard infected fruit and check stored fruit regularly.

PREVENT

Monitor foliage, avoid splashing leaves and fruit, and remove affected plants promptly.

Tomato
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Buckeye Rot
RECOGNISE

Concentric brown rings spread around a grey patch on unripe fruit, often where soil splashes onto low trusses.

ACT

Remove and discard infected fruit.

PREVENT

Support low trusses, use a clean mulch and water carefully at root level.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Ghost Spot
RECOGNISE

Small pale or transparent rings form on fruit after grey-mould spores land on it.

ACT

Superficial ghost spots alone do not spoil otherwise sound fruit; discard any showing rot.

PREVENT

Ventilate well, avoid splashing fruit and remove grey-mould sources.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Magnesium Deficiency

Yellowing between veins

RECOGNISE

Older leaves yellow between green veins and may turn brown. Confirm magnesium deficiency and review feeding.

ACT

Check watering, pH and feeding before seeking an organic-compatible magnesium correction.

PREVENT

Use balanced feeding; excessive potassium can restrict magnesium uptake.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Hormone Damage

Fern-like leaves

RECOGNISE

Twisted, fern-like leaves, distorted stalks and misshapen fruit may follow weedkiller contamination; viruses can look similar.

ACT

Stop exposure and confirm the cause. There is no direct cure.

PREVENT

Keep lawn weedkiller drift, contaminated equipment and suspect compost or manure away from crops.

TOMATO, GREENHOUSE / TOMATO, OUTDOOR

Slugs

Fruit or seedlings eaten near soil level

RECOGNISE

Low fruit and seedlings are eaten, particularly on bush tomatoes close to damp soil.

ACT

Remove spoiled fruit and hand-pick slugs during damp weather or after dark.

PREVENT

Support fruit clear of soil and check low trusses regularly; taller varieties can reduce exposure.

IMPERIAL · 5

Turnip, Swede & Radish
Troubles

Protect young brassica roots from leaf and root feeders, and keep growth steady. Heat, drought and crowding quickly spoil radish quality; swedes stay longer and need checking for internal damage. Harvest tender roots promptly and store only sound ones.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

RADISH

Bolting Winter Radish
RECOGNISE

Winter radishes sown too early may flower instead of swelling into useful roots.

ACT

Pull bolted plants and resow in the correct season if time allows.

PREVENT

Sow winter radishes in July or August, following variety guidance.

TURNIP / SWEDE / RADISH

Bird Damage
RECOGNISE

Birds tear turnip and swede leaves, especially in autumn and winter. Heavy damage checks growth.

ACT

Protect remaining foliage and keep plants growing steadily.

PREVENT

Use securely supported netting where needed, checking regularly for trapped wildlife.

TURNIP / SWEDE / RADISH

Caterpillars
RECOGNISE

Caterpillars eat turnip and swede leaves. Roots may remain usable, but heavy defoliation reduces growth.

ACT

Hand-remove caterpillars and badly damaged leaves where practical.

PREVENT

Protect vulnerable young plants with insect-proof mesh; inspect beneath covers.

RADISH

Woody, Hollow or Soft Radish Roots
RECOGNISE

Summer radishes become pithy, hollow, woody or too hot when overmature or checked by heat, crowding or uneven watering.

ACT

Pull overmature roots; use only tender, sound parts.

PREVENT

Sow little and often, thin early and keep moist. Harvest young; use light shade in hot weather.

TURNIP / SWEDE / RADISH

Flea Beetle

Peppered leaves

RECOGNISE

Small jumping beetles pepper young leaves with tiny holes, especially in late spring and early summer.

ACT

Keep seedlings watered and growing; tolerate small holes on vigorous plants.

PREVENT

Cover early rows with fine mesh or fleece. Quick early or later sowings may escape peak damage.

TURNIP / SWEDE / RADISH

Cabbage Root Fly

Tunnels in roots

RECOGNISE

Cream maggots tunnel in turnip, swede and radish roots. Small roots may be ruined; larger ones sometimes retain sound flesh.

ACT

Trim minor damage from large roots; discard badly affected or rotten roots.

PREVENT

Cover soon after sowing with insect-proof mesh on a rotated bed. Keep growth steady and harvest quick crops promptly.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 1

Turnip, Swede & Radish
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

TURNIP / SWEDE / RADISH

Checked Growth / Poor Root Quality
RECOGNISE

Heat, drought, crowding, poor soil or delayed harvest produces tough, fibrous, split or strong-tasting roots.

ACT

Harvest usable roots promptly and remove failed or overmature rows.

PREVENT

Sow in season, thin early, weed and water steadily. Harvest spring crops young; use cooler autumn conditions.

TURNIP / SWEDE

Soft Rot
RECOGNISE

Wet, slimy decay begins at the crown; foliage collapses while the outer root skin may stay firm. Stored roots can also rot.

ACT

Remove affected plants or stored roots promptly.

PREVENT

Improve drainage, avoid overfeeding and root injuries, rotate crops and never store damaged roots.

TURNIP / SWEDE

Boron Deficiency / Brown Heart

Brown or hollow core

RECOGNISE

Grey-brown areas or rings develop inside turnips and swedes, sometimes with a hollow centre. Rot and other disorders can look similar.

ACT

Existing damage cannot heal. Discard badly affected roots; use only sound flesh.

PREVENT

Confirm deficiency and use soil-test-based advice. Follow the advised rate carefully; excess boron is toxic.

TURNIP / SWEDE / RADISH

Black Rot

Outer black ring

RECOGNISE

Leaves yellow with black veins. Cut roots show a dark ring or dots beneath the skin, often in warm, wet conditions.

ACT

Remove diseased plants; there is no cure.

PREVENT

Rotate crops and provide good drainage.

TURNIP

Turnip Mosaic Virus

Dark green spots

RECOGNISE

Young turnip leaves become twisted and mottled, with raised dark-green patches. Severe infection damages young plants.

ACT

Remove infected plants; there is no cure.

PREVENT

Use healthy plants, monitor aphids and encourage predators. Aphid control cannot guarantee protection.

Bean and Pea
Troubles

Start with the affected part: missing seedlings, marked leaves or damaged pods. Broad beans are prone to blackfly and chocolate spot; peas to weevils, moth caterpillars and mildew. Tender beans need warm soil and steady moisture, particularly at flowering. Not every leaf mark needs treatment.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

PEA / BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER

Seed Beetle

Tunnelled seeds

RECOGNISE

Small round holes in stored pea or bean seeds contain seed-beetle grubs. Damaged seed may fail or give weak plants.

ACT

Do not sow visibly holed seed; there is no useful repair.

PREVENT

Buy good-quality seed and inspect it before sowing.

PEA

Leaf and Pod Spot

Dry spots on pods

RECOGNISE

Sunken brown spots mark pea pods; peas may discolour. Similar stem and leaf spots can merge in severe wet-weather attacks.

ACT

Remove and destroy badly diseased plants.

PREVENT

Rotate crops and clear affected crop remains.

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER / PEA

Mice
RECOGNISE

Seeds or seedlings disappear, often overnight or under cover. Birds and larger animals can leave similar losses.

ACT

Check the pattern of damage before deciding which animal to exclude.

PREVENT

Raise vulnerable seed in pots or modules. Protect outdoor sowings with suitable physical barriers.

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER / PEA

No Flowers
RECOGNISE

Immaturity, shade, drought or excessive nitrogen can delay flowers. Inspect buds for feeding damage.

ACT

Check buds for damage and review feeding rather than adding more nitrogen.

PREVENT

Use balanced nutrition appropriate to the soil, not heavy nitrogen feeding.

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER

Bean Seed Fly

Tunnelled seedlings

RECOGNISE

Grubs tunnel into bean seeds and seedlings. Seeds fail; emerged plants wilt or distort. Early sowings are most vulnerable.

ACT

Remove damaged seedlings.

PREVENT

Prepare a good seedbed, or start plants in compost-filled pots before planting out.

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER / PEA

Birds

Torn pods

RECOGNISE

Pigeons eat seeds and young leaves; sparrows tear pea pods. Birds may pull young beans or damage runner-bean flowers.

ACT

Protect the crop as soon as damage appears.

PREVENT

Use securely supported netting or wire guards; keep it taut, clear of plants and check for trapped wildlife.

Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER

Black Bean Aphid

Aphids on leaves

RECOGNISE

Dense black colonies on soft broad-bean tips can stunt growth and distort flowers and pods. French beans may be affected in midsummer.

ACT

Pinch off infested broad-bean tips; squash small colonies where needed. Allow natural predators time to act.

PREVENT

Pinch broad-bean tops at full flower or after the first pods form. Avoid late sowing where attacks recur.

PEA

Pea Aphid

Aphids on leaves

RECOGNISE

Large aphid colonies can check pea growth and damage flowers, although small numbers rarely cause serious trouble.

ACT

Monitor first; squash damaging colonies by hand and let natural predators help.

PREVENT

Encourage aphid predators and keep checking tender growth. Complete exclusion is rarely practical.

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER / PEA

Pea and Bean Weevil

Notched leaves

RECOGNISE

U-shaped notches appear along young leaf edges. Grey-brown adults drop when disturbed. Established plants usually outgrow the damage.

ACT

Water seedlings in dry weather to support recovery. Severe damage matters most on small plants.

PREVENT

Raise strong plants and protect vulnerable young crops with insect-proof mesh where attacks recur.

PEA

Pea Thrips

Silvery pods

RECOGNISE

Tiny dark or yellowish insects cause silver patches and small holes on leaves and pods. Hot, dry weather favours damaging attacks.

ACT

Check for insects; water stressed plants, encourage predators and tolerate minor damage.

PREVENT

Keep plants watered and growing steadily; clear the crop after harvest.

BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER

No Pods
RECOGNISE

Runner-bean flowers fall without pods after drought or hot weather; cool weather may reduce pollination. French beans can also drop flowers when dry.

ACT

Water roots thoroughly during dry spells, especially from flowering. Check for flower damage by birds.

PREVENT

Maintain root moisture, mulch and water during flowering. Plant after frost risk and protect flowers from damage.

PEA

Pea Moth

Maggoty peas

RECOGNISE

Pale caterpillars feed inside pods, leaving damaged peas and frass. Flowering crops are vulnerable during summer egg laying.

ACT

Once caterpillars enter pods there is no useful treatment. Discard affected peas when shelling.

PREVENT

Use early or late sowings to avoid peak moth activity, or cover with insect-proof mesh before flowering.

Bean and Pea
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

PEA

Marsh Spot

Brown-centred peas

RECOGNISE

A brown-lined cavity inside peas, sometimes with slight yellowing between leaf veins, indicates possible manganese shortage.

ACT

Existing damaged peas cannot be repaired. Confirm the deficiency before adding trace elements.

PREVENT

Improve soil with compost and check pH. Seek advice on an organic-compatible correction if the shortage is confirmed.

BEAN, BROAD

Chocolate Spot

Spots on leaves

RECOGNISE

Chocolate-brown spots on broad-bean leaves can merge; stems, flowers and pods may also be affected. Cool, damp, crowded crops are most at risk.

ACT

Remove badly diseased plants and clear infected remains after cropping.

PREVENT

Improve spacing and airflow. Do not save infected seed; consider spring sowing if autumn crops repeatedly suffer.

BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER

Halo Blight

Spots on leaves

RECOGNISE

Water-soaked leaf spots with yellow halos and wet-looking pod lesions may indicate bacterial halo blight.

ACT

Remove and destroy diseased plants.

PREVENT

Use healthy bought seed. Remove diseased debris, rotate crops and avoid handling wet foliage.

BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER

Anthracnose

Dry spots on pods

RECOGNISE

Sunken dark pod spots, stem cankers and brown leaf patches may develop pinkish margins on French and runner beans.

ACT

Remove badly diseased plants. Confirm the diagnosis before taking further action.

PREVENT

Rotate crops, space for airflow and never save seed from affected plants.

PEA

Downy Mildew

Mouldy leaves

RECOGNISE

Yellow patches above pea leaves correspond to mauve or brown mould below. Cool, wet weather favours infection; pods may distort.

ACT

Remove affected leaves and severely diseased plants.

PREVENT

Rotate crops, reduce crowding and avoid prolonged leaf wetness. Water early if foliage will get wet.

PEA

Powdery Mildew
RECOGNISE

White powdery patches affect leaves and sometimes pods, often on late crops. Dry roots and crowded growth increase stress.

ACT

Remove badly affected growth where practical; clear exhausted late crops.

PREVENT

Maintain root moisture and airflow. Choose resistant varieties for late crops where mildew recurs.

Bean and Pea
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

BEAN, FRENCH / PEA

Grey Mould (Botrytis)

Rotten pods

RECOGNISE

Softly rotting pods or stems develop fuzzy grey mould, especially in wet weather and crowded crops.

ACT

Remove mouldy pods and damaged material promptly.

PREVENT

Keep picking, avoid crowding and improve airflow; minimise prolonged wet foliage.

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER / PEA

Fusarium Wilt

Brown-streaked tissue

RECOGNISE

Stunting, yellow or rolled leaves and poor cropping may accompany reddish-brown streaks inside a cut stem, without outside browning.

ACT

Remove affected plants. Confirm the cause: wilting alone is not a diagnosis.

PREVENT

Choose wilt-resistant varieties where this disease has been confirmed.

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER / PEA

Foot Rot and Root Rot

Blackened stems

RECOGNISE

Leaves yellow and shrivel as roots and stem bases turn brown or black and decay.

ACT

Lift badly affected plants. Rotten roots cannot be restored; improve drainage before replanting.

PREVENT

Rotate crops and avoid conditions that leave roots persistently wet. Investigate recurring losses before replanting.

GROWING GUIDES
METRIC · 4

Beetroot
Troubles

Protect young seedlings and keep roots growing steadily. Check leaf damage, bolting and root quality separately. Confirm nutrient problems before adding trace elements, and lift sound roots before prolonged autumn wet or severe frost.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

BEETROOT

Blackleg
RECOGNISE

Seedlings blacken, shrivel and may collapse. Crowding, poor drainage and excess moisture favour seedling disease.

ACT

Remove collapsed seedlings. Correct excess wetness; affected plants will not recover.

PREVENT

Sow thinly in well-drained ground. For modules, use fresh seed compost and clean trays; avoid overwatering.

BEETROOT

Bolting
RECOGNISE

A flower stem forms before a useful root develops. Cold during early growth or hot, dry conditions can trigger bolting.

ACT

Remove bolted plants; sow replacements when conditions are suitable.

PREVENT

Use Boltardy for protected early sowings, or sow as spring warms. Maintain moisture and thin direct sowings promptly.

BEETROOT

Leaf Spot

Spotted leaves

RECOGNISE

Brown spots may develop pale centres that fall out. Light spotting may have little effect; severe leaf loss can check growth.

ACT

Remove badly affected leaves; minor spotting seldom needs intervention.

PREVENT

Rotate crops and prepare adequately nourished soil before sowing.

BEETROOT

Fanging
RECOGNISE

Roots divide or fork, often where fresh manure, stones or poorly prepared heavy soil interrupt growth.

ACT

Existing forked roots will not straighten.

PREVENT

Use ground manured for a previous crop, or well-rotted compost added in autumn. Remove stones and prepare the soil well.

BEETROOT

Beet Leaf Miner (Mangold Fly)

Blistered leaves

RECOGNISE

White grubs mine leaves, making pale blotches that turn brown. Early summer damage checks young plants; flies are active April–September.

ACT

Remove mined leaves, or crush grubs within mines. Check leaf undersides for clusters of white eggs.

PREVENT

Use insect-proof mesh on a rotated site: overwintering flies can emerge beneath covers on old ground.

METRIC · 1

Beetroot
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

BEETROOT

Heart Rot

Blackened roots

RECOGNISE

Summer wilting, sunken brown root tops and blackened internal flesh can indicate boron deficiency, especially on dry, light or over-limed soil.

ACT

Check soil pH and confirm the shortage. Seek an organic-compatible correction if needed; damaged roots will not recover.

PREVENT

Maintain moisture, add mature compost and avoid unnecessary lime. Excess boron damages plants: never dose by guesswork.

BEETROOT

Autumnal Fungal Root Rots
RECOGNISE

Dark, decaying areas can develop on roots left in wet autumn soil. Appearance alone does not identify the cause.

ACT

Lift promptly. Discard rotting roots and check stored roots regularly.

PREVENT

Lift before prolonged wet or severe frost. Avoid harvest damage and store only sound roots in a cool, frost-free place.

BEETROOT

Speckled Yellows

Rolled leaves

RECOGNISE

Yellow areas between veins may become brown; leaf edges roll inward. Manganese deficiency is one possible cause.

ACT

Check pH and moisture and confirm the cause. Seek an organic-compatible correction if needed; other deficiencies can look similar.

PREVENT

Avoid over-liming; maintain good soil condition and steady growth.

Brassica
Troubles

Check roots as well as leaves when brassicas wilt or stop growing. Mesh, sound transplants and steady growth prevent many losses; disease and nutrient problems need different responses. Test soil before liming or adding trace elements. Cabbage, cauliflower, sprouts and kohl rabi also have distinct quality problems.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

KOHL RABI

Woody Kohl Rabi
RECOGNISE

The swollen stem becomes hard and fibrous after drought, crowding, slow growth or late harvest.

ACT

There is no cure once woody. Use only parts that remain tender.

PREVENT

Grow steadily in fertile, moisture-retentive soil. Space correctly, water in dry spells and harvest young unless using a variety bred for large tender stems.

BROCCOLI / BRUSSELS SPROUTS / CABBAGE / CAULIFLOWER / KALE / KOHL RABI

White Blister (White Rust)
RECOGNISE

Raised white blisters, mainly beneath leaves, may also affect stems or flowers and distort growth.

ACT

Remove affected leaves and reduce crowding.

PREVENT

Avoid repeating brassicas on the affected ground the following season.

BROCCOLI / BRUSSELS SPROUTS / CABBAGE / CAULIFLOWER / KALE / KOHL RABI

Pigeons
RECOGNISE

Soft leaf tissue is stripped away, often leaving stalks and veins. Winter and early spring damage can be severe.

ACT

Cover vulnerable crops promptly; stripped leaves will not repair themselves.

PREVENT

Keep taut netting well clear of foliage and secure the edges. Check frequently for trapped wildlife.

BROCCOLI / BRUSSELS SPROUTS / CABBAGE / CAULIFLOWER / KALE / KOHL RABI

Leaf Spot (Ring Spot)
RECOGNISE

Ringed leaf spots can yellow foliage and cause leaf fall; wet weather favours spread.

ACT

Remove badly affected leaves and improve airflow.

PREVENT

Rotate brassicas; avoid the affected site next season.

BROCCOLI / BRUSSELS SPROUTS / CABBAGE / CAULIFLOWER / KALE / KOHL RABI

Clubroot (Finger and Toe)

Swollen roots

RECOGNISE

Swollen, distorted roots accompany stunting, purple leaves and wilting in sun. Plants may temporarily revive when cooler.

ACT

Remove affected roots; do not home-compost them. There is no cure. Moving brassicas for only a few seasons may be insufficient: soil can remain infected for up to 20 years.

PREVENT

Use clean transplants, improve drainage and consider resistant varieties. Test pH before liming; long rotations do not guarantee clearance.

Large holes in leaves

Small holes in leaves

RECOGNISE

Tiny jumping beetles pepper young leaves with small round holes. Seedlings are most vulnerable in warm spring weather.

ACT

Water damaged seedlings in dry weather so they can outgrow injury.

Protect susceptible young plants with insect-proof mesh. Raise strong transplants where direct sowings repeatedly fail.

Slugs and Snails
RECOGNISE

Irregular feeding holes and seedling losses are worst in damp weather. Look among loose leaves and open sprouts for hidden slugs.

ACT

Inspect after dark or in damp conditions and hand-remove slugs around vulnerable plants.

PREVENT

Raise sturdy transplants. Remove old yellow leaves and damp debris nearby; retain wildlife habitat elsewhere for predators.

Mealy Aphid

Insects on leaves

RECOGNISE

Waxy grey aphid colonies gather under leaves and on tips, often from June. Leaves curl and yellow; heavy colonies can leave sooty mould.

ACT

Check new growth; squash small damaging colonies by hand while leaving natural predators to help.

PREVENT

Remove old brassica stalks after cropping and encourage aphid predators.

Skin-covered holes

PREVENT

Check through summer, especially where previous attacks have occurred; use well-secured insect-proof mesh.

Blind plants

RECOGNISE

Distorted stalks near the growing point and blind growth may indicate swede midge. Look for tiny pale larvae and confirm the cause.

ACT

Remove badly affected plants. Seek confirmation before attributing unexplained blind growth to this uncommon pest.

PREVENT

Check young plants regularly and confirm unexplained growing-point damage.

Downy Mildew
RECOGNISE

Yellow areas above leaves correspond to white down underneath. Crowded young plants in damp conditions can be badly checked.

ACT

Remove affected leaves and severely diseased plants.

Use clean seed compost, avoid crowding and prolonged wet leaves, and use a fresh seedbed after previous trouble.

Tunnelled roots

RECOGNISE

Yellow V-shaped patches spread inward from leaf edges; veins darken and growth is checked. Warm, wet weather favours spread.

ACT

Remove and destroy diseased plants. There is no useful cure in the source.

Use healthy seed and transplants, clear infected debris, rotate and avoid handling wet plants.

Shrunken stems

RECOGNISE

Seedling stem bases blacken and narrow. Plants die or survive with slow growth and brittle stems.

ACT

Badly affected seedlings are not worth planting out.

Swollen roots

ACT

Monitor affected plants; severe damage needs a fresh diagnosis.

Cutworm

Severed stems

RECOGNISE

Grey or brown caterpillars hide just below the surface and sever young stems at ground level, often in June and July.

ACT

Hoe around affected plants and collect caterpillars exposed near damaged stems.

PREVENT

Where repeated losses occur, consider an appropriate nematode product, following its temperature and moisture instructions.

CABBAGE

Heartless Cabbages
RECOGNISE

Drought, poor fertility, shade, crowding or root damage can prevent firm heads. Check establishment and variety.

ACT

Check moisture and feeding; use balanced nutrition rather than adding straight nitrogen.

PREVENT

Choose a suitable sunny site, prepare fertile firm ground and plant securely.

CABBAGE

Split Hearts
RECOGNISE

Hearts split when rapid growth follows a check, particularly rain after drought. Freezing and thawing can also damage winter heads.

ACT

Harvest mature split heads promptly; do not expect the split to heal.

PREVENT

Keep moisture steady and avoid leaving mature heads standing too long, especially before severe cold.

BRUSSELS SPROUTS

Blown Brussels Sprouts
RECOGNISE

Sprouts become open and leafy rather than tight buttons. Loose soil, drought, crowding and other growth checks contribute.

ACT

Pick small tender blown sprouts for prompt use; remove larger spoiled ones.

PREVENT

Firm plants well, give adequate space and water in dry weather. An F1 variety may produce firmer sprouts.

CAULIFLOWER

Button Cauliflowers
RECOGNISE

Very small heads form early and soon run to seed after checks to growth. Pests, poor soil, crowding, drought or nutrient shortages may contribute.

ACT

Established button heads will not become normal full-sized curds.

PREVENT

Use rich firm soil, proper spacing and hardened-off plants. Water consistently and prevent early pest damage. Investigate suspected deficiencies before treatment.

CAULIFLOWER

Whiptail

Narrow leaves

RECOGNISE

Thin, strap-like cauliflower leaves and very small or absent heads suggest molybdenum deficiency, often associated with acid soil.

ACT

Confirm the cause and test soil pH; seek advice on an organic-compatible correction if needed.

PREVENT

Test pH and correct excessive acidity before the next cauliflower crop.

Troubles

CAULIFLOWER

Boron Deficiency

Brown curds

RECOGNISE

Cauliflower leaves distort; curds may be small, brown-spotted or bitter. These signs alone do not confirm boron shortage.

ACT

Confirm the deficiency and check pH and moisture. Seek an organic-compatible correction; damaged curds will not repair themselves.

PREVENT

Improve soil with compost and keep growth steady. Excess boron is toxic: never dose by guesswork.

BROCCOLI / BRUSSELS SPROUTS / CABBAGE / CAULIFLOWER / KALE / KOHL RABI

Magnesium Deficiency

Mottling between veins

RECOGNISE

Older leaves develop yellowing between veins, sometimes followed by reddish or brown areas.

ACT

Confirm the problem and check watering, pH and feeding. Seek advice on a suitable organic-compatible magnesium amendment if needed.

PREVENT

Improve light soil with compost. Avoid excessive potassium feeding, which can reduce magnesium uptake.

BROCCOLI / BRUSSELS SPROUTS / CABBAGE / CAULIFLOWER / KALE / KOHL RABI

Frost

Cold-damaged leaves

RECOGNISE

Severe cold damages exposed heads and leaves, especially where plants are loose. Winter cabbages and savoys tolerate some frost.

ACT

Allow healthy growing points to recover. Remove rotting leaves and gently re-firm lifted roots.

PREVENT

Plant securely and earth up where needed. Harvest sound mature heads before severe weather when appropriate.

BROCCOLI / BRUSSELS SPROUTS / CABBAGE / CAULIFLOWER / KALE / KOHL RABI

Cabbage Stem Flea Beetle

Tunnelled stems

RECOGNISE

Wilting plants may have cream-coloured grubs inside stems. Attacks occur mainly from August to October.

ACT

Remove badly infested plants after checking inside stems to confirm the cause.

PREVENT

Rotate away from affected ground rather than repeating brassicas there next season.

BROCCOLI / BRUSSELS SPROUTS / CABBAGE / CAULIFLOWER / KALE / KOHL RABI

Manganese Deficiency
RECOGNISE

Yellowing between veins with curled or scorched edges can resemble other nutrient problems; one leaf is not enough for a firm diagnosis.

ACT

Check soil conditions and confirm the cause. Seek advice on an organic-compatible correction if required.

PREVENT

Maintain good soil condition and avoid unnecessary liming.

Carrot and Parsnip
Troubles

Carrots and parsnips share several root pests and diseases. Carrots are especially vulnerable to carrot fly; parsnips also suffer from old seed and canker. Start with fresh seed, deep well-prepared soil and a clean seedbed. Avoid fresh manure; use resistant varieties where available.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

PARSNIP

Old Seed / Poor Germination
RECOGNISE

Old seed, cold or dry soil and deep sowing can all delay or prevent emergence. Check conditions before resowing.

ACT

Sow again with fresh seed if the season still allows.

PREVENT

Use fresh seed each year. Keep the drill moist until seedlings emerge; a few radish seeds can mark the row.

CARROT

Green Top
RECOGNISE

Sunlight turns exposed carrot crowns green. Unlike green potatoes, green carrots are not harmful, but look unsightly.

PREVENT

Earth up around exposed crowns during the growing season.

PARSNIP

Parsnip Rust Fungus
RECOGNISE

Rust-coloured crown damage may resemble staining or canker; the precise cause needs confirmation.

ACT

Lift and discard badly affected roots.

PREVENT

Improve drainage, avoid root injury and seek a diagnosis before choosing a long crop break.

CARROT

Clayburn
RECOGNISE

Carrot surface damage associated with clay; check for pests or rot. The cause is uncertain.

ACT

Inspect affected roots; seek identification for recurring damage. Discard active decay.

PREVENT

Prepare well-drained, workable soil; use a raised bed where necessary.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Carrot Fly

Tunnelled roots

RECOGNISE

Leaves turn reddish, then yellow. Maggots tunnel in carrots or damage parsnip surfaces. Seedlings may die; roots may rot.

ACT

No cure. Minor surface damage on large parsnips may be trimmed away.

PREVENT

Cover completely with insect-proof mesh on rotated ground. Sow thinly. Carrots sown after mid-May or lifted before late August may avoid peak attacks.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Fanging

Forked roots

RECOGNISE

Roots fork when tips meet stones, compaction or injury. Fresh manure and uneven seedbeds can contribute.

ACT

There is no treatment for an already forked root.

PREVENT

Prepare workable soil, remove larger stones and avoid compaction or fresh manure before sowing.

Carrot and Parsnip
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

CARROT

Small Roots
RECOGNISE

Crowding, drought, poor soil or pest damage can keep roots small. First check variety and maturity.

ACT

Check spacing, water and root health. Thin carefully and correct confirmed poor fertility.

PREVENT

Prepare workable soil in advance; maintain suitable spacing and steady moisture.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Splitting

Split roots

RECOGNISE

Roots split after heavy rain or watering follows a dry spell. Leaving mature roots in wet autumn soil also increases the risk.

ACT

There is no cure. Use split roots immediately; they will not store.

PREVENT

Water regularly and deeply in drought. Mulch with compost to steady moisture. Where splitting recurs, lift maincrop carrots before prolonged wet weather.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Sclerotinia Rot

Mouldy roots

RECOGNISE

Soft root or crown rot develops white cottony mould, sometimes with black resting bodies. Both growing crops and stored roots can be affected.

ACT

Remove infected plants and rotten stored roots promptly; keep them out of home compost.

PREVENT

Store sound roots and check regularly. Clear infected debris, improve drainage and avoid moving contaminated soil.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Carrot-Willow Aphid

Distorted leaves

RECOGNISE

Greenfly cause distorted, discoloured, stunted leaves, especially in warm, dry summers. They can also transmit motley dwarf virus.

ACT

Tolerate small colonies; squash damaging colonies and encourage natural predators.

PREVENT

Inspect young crops and maintain steady growth. Aphid management cannot guarantee protection from viruses.

CARROT

Black Rot

Blackened carrot roots

RECOGNISE

Large black patches develop on stored carrots, often with no obvious symptoms before harvest.

ACT

Remove and destroy diseased roots promptly.

PREVENT

Store only sound roots in a cool, ventilated place and inspect regularly. Do not grow carrots on the same land next year. Avoid reusing a problem storage site year after year.

CARROT

Carrot Motley Dwarf

Discoloured leaves

RECOGNISE

Yellow mottling, red outer leaves and stunting may indicate carrot motley dwarf, an aphid-transmitted virus complex.

ACT

Confirm the cause and remove badly affected plants; infected plants cannot be cured.

PREVENT

Inspect young growth, encourage aphid predators and remove damaging colonies. Virus spread can still occur.

Troubles

PARSNIP

Parsnip Canker

Blackened parsnip roots

RECOGNISE

Brown or black rot and cracking around the crown. Damage can spread downwards in wet, heavy soil; large roots suffer most.

ACT

No cure. Trim damage and use sound roots promptly. Destroy badly rotten roots; do not store them.

PREVENT

Choose resistant varieties such as Gladiator, White Gem or Avonresister. Test pH before liming; avoid fresh manure or unfinished compost. Prepare well-drained soil. Where canker recurs, sow later for smaller roots.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Violet Root Rot

Mouldy roots

RECOGNISE

Foliage may yellow slightly. Lifted roots show a felt-like coating of purple fungal threads, especially on the lower parts.

ACT

There is no cure. Destroy diseased roots.

PREVENT

Keep affected roots out of storage. Remove infected roots, avoid moving soil and seek crop-break advice if losses recur.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Swift Moth

Hollowed-out roots

RECOGNISE

Soil-living caterpillars hollow out roots and may move backwards when disturbed. Affected plants can lose vigour.

ACT

Inspect soil beside damaged roots; hand-remove caterpillars. Discard badly damaged or rotting roots.

PREVENT

Check vulnerable plants. For recurring losses, consider suitable biological nematodes with supplier guidance.

Celery
Troubles

Keep celery and celeriac growing steadily: moist roots, good drainage and healthy seedlings matter. Check leaves for miners and spots, and inspect stalks and hearts for damage. Celery needs moisture, but wet, crowded conditions can also favour disease.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

CELERY / CELERIAC

Bolting
RECOGNISE

Cold exposure or checks during young growth can trigger premature flowering in celery or celeriac.

ACT

There is no way to reverse bolting.

PREVENT

Keep roots moist, harden plants gradually and wait until frost risk has passed before planting.

CELERY

Splitting

Split stalks

RECOGNISE

Vertical splits spoil stalks after dry soil, uneven growth or excessive nitrogen.

ACT

Existing splits cannot heal.

PREVENT

Water steadily, improve soil with mature compost and avoid excessive nitrogen feeding.

CELERY / CELERIAC

Damping Off
RECOGNISE

Seedlings develop a watery, soft stem base and topple over, often in wet, poorly aired trays.

ACT

Remove affected seedlings; improve ventilation and avoid splashing the remainder.

PREVENT

Sow thinly in clean compost. Keep it just damp, air trays and remove condensation from covers.

CELERY / CELERIAC

Celery Leaf Spot (Blight)

Spotted leaves

RECOGNISE

Brown or yellow-brown spots start on outer leaflets and spread in wet conditions. Infection can arrive on seed or seedlings.

ACT

Remove affected leaves and discard badly diseased plants.

PREVENT

Buy healthy seed and plants. Reject spotted seedlings; allow airflow and avoid splashing foliage.

CELERY / CELERIAC

Celery Fly (Leaf Miner)

Blistered leaves

RECOGNISE

Broad pale leaf mines dry into brown papery blotches. Young celery may become stunted and bitter; celeriac is also affected.

ACT

Tolerate light damage; pinch out badly mined leaf parts on uncovered plants.

PREVENT

Check young plants from May. Use insect-proof mesh on a rotated bed, so flies cannot emerge beneath it.

CELERY

Celery Heart Rot

Rotten hearts

RECOGNISE

The inner heart becomes a slimy brown mass. Wounds from slugs, frost or cultivation allow bacterial rot to enter.

ACT

Discard diseased plants; rotten hearts cannot recover.

PREVENT

Keep roots evenly moist but well drained. Avoid wounds and burying the heart; rotate away from a previously affected bed.

CELERY / CELERIAC

Slugs and Snails
RECOGNISE

Irregular holes spoil celery stalks; celeriac roots may also be holed. Woodlice sometimes occupy existing damage.

ACT

Hand-remove slugs after dark. At harvest, trim damage and use sound tissue promptly; discard rot.

PREVENT

Keep damp debris away from vulnerable plants, check regularly and harvest before damage becomes severe.

Cucurbit
Troubles

Cucumbers, courgettes, marrows and squash need warmth and steady moisture, but dislike cold, waterlogged roots. Check pollination before blaming disease for poor fruit set. Under glass, balance humidity with ventilation; handle storage squash carefully.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

CUCUMBER, GREENHOUSE / CUCUMBER, OUTDOOR / COURGETTES AND MARROWS / SQUASHES AND PUMPKINS

No Fruit
RECOGNISE

Poor pollination, cold or root stress can limit fruit set. Check cucumber variety needs.

ACT

On a dry morning, transfer pollen from a male flower to female flowers. Keep roots moist.

PREVENT

Do not apply this to greenhouse cucumbers grown for unpollinated fruit; follow the variety instructions.

CUCUMBER, GREENHOUSE

Poor Yield
RECOGNISE

Greenhouse cucumbers may lose vigour after the first harvest, especially if fruit becomes over-mature or roots are stressed.

ACT

Pick frequently, water steadily and feed at the recommended rate. Keep mulch clear of the stem base and check drainage.

PREVENT

Maintain warmth, steady moisture and healthy roots; do not leave mature fruit on the plant.

CUCUMBER, GREENHOUSE / CUCUMBER, OUTDOOR / COURGETTES AND MARROWS / SQUASHES AND PUMPKINS

Withering of Young Fruit
RECOGNISE

Young fruit stops swelling and shrivels. Check pollination needs, root health and temperatures.

ACT

Remove failed fruit. Check soil moisture and drainage before watering; do not impose a fixed dry week.

PREVENT

Keep growth steady and protect roots from cold, drought and waterlogging.

CUCUMBER, GREENHOUSE / CUCUMBER, OUTDOOR / COURGETTES AND MARROWS / SQUASHES AND PUMPKINS

Sun Scald

Papery patches

RECOGNISE

Pale brown, papery patches develop at leaf margins after excessive sun; dry tissue shrinks.

ACT

Scorched tissue will not recover.

PREVENT

Provide greenhouse shading and ventilation while keeping roots evenly moist.

CUCUMBER, GREENHOUSE / CUCUMBER, OUTDOOR / COURGETTES AND MARROWS / SQUASHES AND PUMPKINS

Bitterness
RECOGNISE

Stress can make cucumbers bitter. Unwanted pollination affects some greenhouse varieties; outdoor types have different requirements.

ACT

Do not eat unusually bitter cucumbers, courgettes or squash. Discard them; cutting, rubbing or cooking is not a reliable remedy.

PREVENT

Follow cucumber variety instructions: keep seedless greenhouse crops unpollinated; retain male flowers where outdoor types need pollen. Keep growth steady.

White powdery mould

RECOGNISE

White powdery patches cover leaves or stems, often on older leaves in late summer.

Remove badly affected older leaves and keep the remaining crop growing steadily.

Maintain root moisture, ventilate under glass and choose resistant varieties where available.

Silky webbing

Spots on leaves

RECOGNISE

Pale leaf spots enlarge and turn brown with yellow margins. They may merge; stem lesions can develop pink growth, then darken.

Use clean containers and fresh compost; ventilate and avoid splashing foliage.

Blotch

Spots on leaves

RECOGNISE

Small, pale spots spread across cucumber leaves and can lead to decay. Confirm persistent symptoms.

ACT

Remove badly affected leaves and plants; confirm the cause if it recurs.

PREVENT

Use clean containers and fresh compost, with good airflow and careful watering.

RECOGNISE

Keep fruit clear of soil and avoid water splashing onto it.

Gummosis
RECOGNISE

ACT

Discard diseased fruit and reduce excessive humidity.

Keep the greenhouse suitably warm and well ventilated.

Mould at stem end

RECOGNISE

Root troubles

RECOGNISE

Collapsed stems

RECOGNISE

PREVENT

Avoid waterlogging and keep irrigation away from the stem base.

Root troubles

Soft-skinned fruit

Florence Fennel
Troubles

Florence fennel needs steady growth to form juicy bulbs. Check sowing time and root moisture first. Harvest mature bulbs promptly: prolonged damp and frost can spoil their outer sheaths.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

FLORENCE FENNEL

Bolting / Stemmy Bulbs
RECOGNISE

A narrow bulb elongates into a flowering stem instead of swelling. Once stemmy, it is unlikely to become fleshy.

ACT

Harvest usable parts promptly, trimming tough stems.

PREVENT

For outdoor UK sowing, June or July is usually safer. Choose a bolt-resistant variety and avoid drought or crowding.

FLORENCE FENNEL

Dry Soil / Checked Growth
RECOGNISE

Dry soil checks growth, leaving small, less juicy bulbs and increasing the risk of bolting.

ACT

Water thoroughly and mulch. Harvest small usable bulbs if growth has stalled.

PREVENT

Use moisture-retentive soil, thin promptly and water steadily as bulbs swell. A 5 cm / 2 in compost mulch can help.

FLORENCE FENNEL

Lower Sheath Rot
RECOGNISE

Outer bulb sheaths can soften and rot in wet conditions or after delayed harvest. Check inside before use.

ACT

Lift promptly. Discard rotten tissue; use only firm, sound parts and discard extensively rotted bulbs.

PREVENT

Avoid waterlogging and harvest mature bulbs before prolonged damp causes deterioration.

FLORENCE FENNEL

Frost Damage
RECOGNISE

Exposed bulbs lose quality after frost and may become water-soaked or soft. They do not store well.

ACT

Lift promptly and use only sound flesh; discard soft or rotten bulbs.

PREVENT

Harvest before hard frost. Keep sound harvested bulbs cool and frost-free for short-term use.

Lettuce
Troubles

Keep lettuce growing steadily and check both leaves and roots when plants wilt. Damp, crowded crops favour moulds; dry roots encourage checks and bolting. Endive also needs watching for slugs, especially around blanched hearts.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

LETTUCE

Bolting
RECOGNISE

Long days, heat, drought or other growth checks can trigger early flowering; susceptibility varies by variety.

ACT

Remove unusable bolted plants and compost them.

PREVENT

Transplant promptly and carefully; thin young plants and keep roots evenly moist.

LETTUCE / ENDIVE

Ring Spot

Holed leaves

RECOGNISE

Small brown spots give outer leaves a rusty look; centres may fall out and midribs develop rusty streaks, especially in winter crops.

ACT

Remove affected leaves and discard badly infected plants.

PREVENT

Rotate outdoor crops and ventilate protected plants.

LETTUCE

No Hearts
RECOGNISE

A hearting variety remains open and loose. Crowding, drought, shade or pests may be involved; loose-leaf varieties naturally stay open.

ACT

Check the variety and growing conditions; use sound loose leaves.

PREVENT

Allow room, water steadily and improve soil with compost. Compost alone does not guarantee a heart.

LETTUCE / ENDIVE

Tipburn

Brown-edged leaves

RECOGNISE

Leaf edges turn brown and scorched. Weather, variety and nutrition can contribute; it is not simply an infectious leaf spot.

ACT

Damaged edges cannot recover. Discard decayed tissue.

PREVENT

Avoid growth checks: keep roots evenly moist and ventilate protected crops.

LETTUCE / ENDIVE

Downy Mildew

White mouldy leaves

RECOGNISE

Yellow patches between veins have white fuzzy mould beneath. Affected tissue turns brown, especially in cool, wet weather.

ACT

Remove infected leaves promptly; discard badly affected plants.

PREVENT

Rotate crops, avoid crowding and ventilate plants under cover.

LETTUCE / ENDIVE

Slugs and Snails
RECOGNISE

Ragged holes, damaged stems and slime trails show night feeding. Young lettuce and endive are especially vulnerable.

ACT

Check after dark or in damp weather and hand-remove slugs and snails.

PREVENT

Keep damp debris away from vulnerable plants and inspect young crops regularly.

Lettuce
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

LETTUCE / ENDIVE

Root Aphid

Damaged roots

RECOGNISE

Roots carry greyish aphids and white waxy deposits. Plants become stunted, yellow or wilted, often in late summer.

ACT

Remove badly declining plants and keep remaining roots moist.

PREVENT

Water in dry weather; look for varieties sold as resistant if attacks recur.

LETTUCE

Eelworm

Damaged roots

RECOGNISE

Root-knot nematodes can cause pale, stunted growth and wilting. Lift a plant to check for gall-like swellings on roots.

ACT

Remove badly affected plants and seek confirmation of the cause.

PREVENT

Avoid spreading affected soil. Plan crop changes around the identified nematode, not a fixed waiting period.

LETTUCE / ENDIVE

Aphid

Greenfly on leaves

RECOGNISE

Colonies cause curled leaves and sticky honeydew; aphids can also spread mosaic virus.

ACT

Squash small colonies or rinse them from leaves where practical.

PREVENT

Encourage natural predators and inspect young plants; aphid control cannot guarantee virus prevention.

LETTUCE / ENDIVE

Grey Mould (Botrytis)

Rotten stems

RECOGNISE

Grey fuzz develops on damaged tissue. Reddish-brown stem rot causes wilting or collapse at soil level in cool, humid conditions.

ACT

Remove diseased plants and improve ventilation.

PREVENT

Handle seedlings gently, keep leaf bases above soil and remove dead leaves.

LETTUCE

Cutworm

Severed stems

RECOGNISE

Large grey, green or brown caterpillars sever young plants at soil level at night. Older roots may be gnawed; June-July is a risk period.

ACT

Search soil beside damaged plants and hand-remove caterpillars.

PREVENT

Check vulnerable young crops; use biological controls only when suitable for the pest and soil conditions.

LETTUCE

Lettuce Root Maggot

Tunnelled roots

RECOGNISE

Root-tunnelling larvae may cause lettuce wilt and stunting. Inspect roots and confirm the insect.

ACT

Remove affected plants. Seek identification: other root problems cause similar wilting.

PREVENT

Inspect unexplained wilt, clear affected debris and use healthy plants and clean growing media.
